An investigation of Haar-random quantum codes reveals a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and nondecodable phases of quantum codes under local noise.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020328] Published Wed May 13, 2026.
tldr: This paper investigates Haar-random quantum codes and identifies a simple mechanism for the transition between decodable and non-decodable phases under local noise.
motivation: Understanding the robustness of quantum error-correcting codes against local noise is crucial for practical quantum computing. The paper aims to characterize the spectral properties and coding transitions of random quantum codes.
method: The authors analyze Haar-random quantum codes using statistical physics methods, mapping the decoding problem to a statistical mechanics model and studying its phase transitions.
result: They find a sharp transition between decodable and non-decodable phases as a function of noise strength, and characterize the spectral properties of the code's density matrix.
conclusion: The results provide insight into the fundamental limits of quantum error correction and suggest that random codes can achieve optimal thresholds under certain conditions.

title: Quantum Cryptography Beyond Key Distribution: Theory And Experiment
authors: Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, And Philip Walther
abstract:
Author(s): Mathieu Bozzio, Claude Crépeau, Petros Wallden, and Philip Walther

Cryptography not only involves the sending of secret messages but also encompasses many protocols and procedures that provide privacy and security in the networked world. Likewise, quantum resources have the potential to enhance cryptography in ways that go beyond the well-known example of quantum key distribution. This review offers a classification of the main crypto primitives that are available quantum mechanically. It explains the security that they offer, including the sometimes significant limitations on their theoretical capabilities. Implementations using current photonic techniques are discussed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045006] Published Fri Dec 19, 2025.
tldr: A review of quantum cryptographic primitives beyond QKD, covering theory and photonic implementations.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive classification and security analysis of quantum cryptography protocols beyond key distribution, addressing the need for a structured overview.
method: The paper reviews and categorizes various quantum cryptographic primitives, explains their security guarantees and limitations, and discusses current photonic implementations.
result: It offers a taxonomy of quantum cryptographic protocols, highlighting their theoretical capabilities and practical challenges in photonic systems.
conclusion: Quantum cryptography extends well beyond QKD, but many protocols have significant limitations; photonic implementations are advancing but face scalability and efficiency issues.

title: Quantum-information Methods For Quantum Gravity Laboratory-based Tests
authors: Chiara Marletto And Vlatko Vedral
abstract:
Author(s): Chiara Marletto and Vlatko Vedral

It is conceptually possible that gravity is a force of nature that is not describable with a classical theory, but is also not described by a conventional quantum theory. Information-theoretic approaches make it possible to address this general idea in a concrete way, with thought experiments that would constrain the scope of whatever new theory emerges. This review gives the status of these new theoretical approaches, with an emphasis on proposed experiments that look for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) between two probes for which quantum theory is known to be applicable. Various potentially feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments that have been proposed are concretely analyzed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015006] Published Fri Mar 14, 2025.
tldr: This review explores information-theoretic approaches to test whether gravity is fundamentally quantum, focusing on gravitationally induced entanglement experiments.
motivation: To constrain possible theories of quantum gravity using quantum information methods, particularly through tabletop experiments that probe the quantum nature of gravity.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks for gravitationally induced entanglement (GIE) and analyzes proposed experimental setups that would detect entanglement between two probes mediated by gravity.
result: Several feasible tabletop-scale GIE experiments are identified and analyzed, showing that quantum information theory can provide concrete experimental tests for quantum gravity.
conclusion: Information-theoretic approaches offer a promising path to experimentally test the quantum nature of gravity, with GIE experiments being a key candidate.

title: Active Quantum Reservoir Engineering: Using A Qubit To Manipulate Its Environment
authors: Marcelo Janovitch, Matteo Brunelli, And Patrick P. Potts
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2143 (2026).

Quantum reservoir engineering leverages dissipative processes to achieve desired behaviour, with applications ranging from entanglement generation to quantum error correction. Therein, a structured environment acts as an entropy sink for the system and no time-dependent control over the system is required. We develop a theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering, where time-dependent control over a quantum system is used to manipulate its environment. In this case, the system may act as an entropy sink for the environment. Our framework captures the dynamical interplay between system and environment, and provides an intuitive picture of how finite-size effects and system-environment correlations allow for manipulating the environment by repeated initialisation of the quantum system. We illustrate our results with two examples: a superconducting qubit coupled to an environment of two-level systems and a semiconducting quantum dot coupled to nuclear spins. In both scenarios, we find qualitative agreement with previous experimental results, illustrating how active control can unlock new functionalities in open quantum systems.

.
tldr: A theoretical framework for active reservoir engineering where time-dependent control over a quantum system manipulates its environment, illustrated with superconducting qubit and quantum dot examples.
motivation: Standard quantum reservoir engineering uses structured environments as entropy sinks, but active control can unlock new functionalities by allowing the system to act as an entropy sink for the environment.
method: The authors develop a framework capturing the dynamical interplay between system and environment, including finite-size effects and correlations, and apply it to two physical systems.
result: Qualitative agreement with previous experimental results is found, demonstrating that repeated initialization of the qubit can manipulate the environment.
conclusion: Active control in open quantum systems enables new functionalities for quantum thermodynamics and information processing.

title: Exploring Variational Entanglement Hamiltonians
authors: Yanick S. Kind And Benedikt Fauseweh
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2133 (2026).

Recent advances in analog and digital quantum-simulation platforms have enabled exploration of the spectrum of entanglement Hamiltonians via variational algorithms. In this work we analyze the convergence properties of the variationally obtained solutions and compare them to numerically exact calculations in quantum critical systems. We demonstrate that interpreting the cost functional as an integral permits the deployment of iterative quadrature schemes, thereby reducing the required number of measurements by more than an order of magnitude even in the presence of noise. We further show that a modified ansatz captures deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form in lattice models, improves convergence, improves trainability and provides a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions. Finally, we establish that a low cost value does not by itself guarantee convergence in trace distance. Nevertheless, it faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps, which are essential for applications to topological phases.

.
tldr: This paper analyzes variational algorithms for extracting entanglement Hamiltonians in quantum critical systems, demonstrating improved convergence and reduced measurements.
motivation: Understanding entanglement Hamiltonians is crucial for characterizing quantum phases and correlations, but their experimental extraction is challenging.
method: The authors interpret the cost functional as an integral to deploy iterative quadrature schemes, and introduce a modified ansatz to capture deviations from the Bisognano-Wichmann form.
result: The approach reduces required measurements by over an order of magnitude, improves convergence and trainability, and provides a cost-function-level diagnostic for quantum phase transitions.
conclusion: Low cost value does not guarantee convergence in trace distance, but faithfully reproduces degeneracies and spectral gaps essential for topological phases.

title: Classical Shadows For Sample-efficient Measurements Of Gauge-invariant Observables
authors: Jacob Bringewatt, Henry Froland, Andreas Elben, And Niklas Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2127 (2026).

Classical shadows provide a versatile framework for estimating many properties of quantum states from repeated, randomly chosen measurements without requiring full quantum state tomography. When prior information is available, such as knowledge of symmetries of states and operators, this knowledge can be exploited to significantly improve sample efficiency. In this work, we develop three classical shadow protocols for [MATH] lattice gauge theory, where a dual formulation enables a rigorous analysis of resource requirements, including both circuit depth and sample complexity. Our approaches can offer exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, albeit at the cost of increased circuit complexity. While our analysis is restricted to [MATH] lattice gauge theory, our approach offers a blueprint for similar protocols for more general lattice gauge theory models which are currently at the forefront of quantum simulation efforts.

.
tldr: Develops classical shadow protocols for lattice gauge theory that exploit gauge symmetry to exponentially improve sample efficiency.
motivation: Estimating gauge-invariant observables in lattice gauge theories is crucial for quantum simulation but sample-inefficient without symmetry exploitation.
method: Proposes three classical shadow protocols that incorporate gauge symmetry via a dual formulation, analyzing circuit depth and sample complexity.
result: Achieves exponential improvements in sample complexity over symmetry-agnostic methods, with trade-offs in circuit complexity.
conclusion: Provides a blueprint for symmetry-enhanced classical shadows in more general lattice gauge theories, advancing quantum simulation capabilities.

title: What Can We Do In A Symmetry-constrained Perspective? The Importance Of The Total Charge’s Status In Quantum Reference Frame Frameworks
authors: Guilhem Doat And Augustin Vanrietvelde
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2126 (2026).

The study of quantum reference frames has received renewed interest over the last years, leading to the parallel development of non-equivalent frameworks by different communities. We clarify the differences between these frameworks. At the mathematical level, they mainly differ in the kind of symmetry (either weak or strong) employed to constrain the system. We show that this mathematical difference corresponds to a fundamental physical question: whether the global charge associated to the symmetry group is accessible to symmetry-constrained observers. In this context, we formulate a definition of a perspective in terms of operational capacities, or lack thereof. Turning to consequences of adopting either approach, we discuss how adopting the weak approach induces an ambiguity in the momenta included in each perspective and bars from defining reversible QRF transformations. We then review and analyze the existing arguments motivating each approach, and show how they bear upon the problem of charge accessibility. Finally, we introduce a simple operational scenario in which upholding two reasonable physical postulates leads to the conclusion that internal observers could measure the global charge by 1/ performing a relativized interference measurement and 2/ classically communicating.

.
tldr: This paper clarifies differences between quantum reference frame frameworks based on weak vs. strong symmetry constraints, linking them to the accessibility of global charge.
motivation: Quantum reference frames are studied in non-equivalent frameworks; the paper aims to resolve the mathematical and physical distinctions between them.
method: The authors analyze weak and strong symmetry constraints, define perspectives in terms of operational capacities, and introduce a scenario where internal observers measure global charge via relativized interference and classical communication.
result: The weak approach induces ambiguity in momenta and prevents reversible QRF transformations; the strong approach allows charge measurement by internal observers under certain postulates.
conclusion: The choice of symmetry constraint corresponds to whether the global charge is accessible, with implications for QRF transformations and operational scenarios.

title: Exact Distinguishability Between Real-valued And Complex-valued Haar Random Quantum States
authors: Tristan Nemoz, Romain Alléaume, And Peter Brown
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2120 (2026).

Haar random states are fundamental objects in quantum information theory and quantum computing. We study the density matrix resulting from sampling [MATH] copies of a [MATH]-dimensional quantum state according to the Haar measure on the orthogonal group. In particular, we analytically compute its spectral decomposition. This allows us to compute exactly the trace distance between [MATH]-copies of a real Haar random state and [MATH]-copies of a complex Haar random state. Using this we show a lower-bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state [MATH]-designs and improve the lower-bound on the number of copies required for imaginarity testing.

.
tldr: This paper analytically computes the spectral decomposition of density matrices from Haar random states on the orthogonal group and uses it to exactly distinguish real vs. complex Haar random states, with implications for state designs and imaginarity testing.
motivation: Understanding the difference between real and complex random quantum states is fundamental for quantum information theory and quantum computing, particularly for state designs and imaginarity.
method: The authors analytically compute the spectral decomposition of the density matrix resulting from sampling multiple copies of a Haar random state on the orthogonal group, then compute the trace distance between real and complex Haar random states.
result: They obtain an exact expression for the trace distance and use it to derive a lower bound on the approximation parameter of real-valued state designs and improve the lower bound on copies needed for imaginarity testing.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous distinction between real and complex random states, advancing the theory of state designs and quantum state distinguishability.

title: On The Dynamical Lie Algebras Of Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithms
authors: Jonathan Allcock, Miklos Santha, Pei Yuan, And Shengyu Zhang
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2119 (2026).

Dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) have emerged as a valuable tool in the study of parameterized quantum circuits, helping to characterize both their expressiveness and trainability. In particular, the absence or presence of barren plateaus (BPs) – flat regions in parameter space that prevent the efficient training of variational quantum algorithms – has recently been shown to be intimately related to quantities derived from the associated DLA. In this work, we investigate DLAs for the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), one of the most studied variational quantum algorithms for solving graph MaxCut and other combinatorial optimization problems. While DLAs for QAOA circuits have been studied before, existing results have either been based on numerical evidence, or else correspond to DLA generators specifically chosen to be universal for quantum computation on a subspace of states. We initiate an analytical study of barren plateaus and other statistics of QAOA algorithms, and give bounds on the dimensions of the corresponding DLAs and their centers for general graphs. We then focus on the [MATH]-vertex cycle and complete graphs. For the cycle graph we give an explicit basis, identify its decomposition into the direct sum of a [MATH]-dimensional center and a semisimple component isomorphic to [MATH] copies of [MATH]. We give an explicit basis for this isomorphism, and a closed-form expression for the variance of the cost function, proving the absence of BPs. For the complete graph we prove that the dimension of the DLA is [MATH] and give an explicit basis for the DLA.

.
tldr: This paper analytically studies dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs) for QAOA circuits, providing bounds on DLA dimensions and proving absence of barren plateaus for cycle graphs.
motivation: Understanding the expressiveness and trainability of variational quantum algorithms like QAOA is crucial; DLAs help characterize barren plateaus, but prior results were numerical or limited to universal generators.
method: The authors analytically bound DLA dimensions and centers for general graphs, then explicitly compute DLAs for cycle and complete graphs using Lie algebra decomposition.
result: For cycle graphs, the DLA decomposes into a center and semisimple component isomorphic to copies of su(2), yielding a closed-form variance of the cost function and proving no barren plateaus. For complete graphs, the DLA dimension is n^2-1 with an explicit basis.
conclusion: The work provides rigorous analytical tools for studying QAOA landscapes, showing that certain graph structures avoid barren plateaus, which is important for practical quantum optimization.

title: Catalytic Entanglement Transformations With Noisy Hardware
authors: Hemant Sharma, Aleksandr Mokeev, Jonas Helsen, And Johannes Borregaard
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2117 (2026).

The availability of certain entangled resource states (catalyst states) can enhance the rate of converting several less entangled states into fewer highly entangled states in a process known as catalytic entanglement concentration (EC). Here, we extend catalytic EC from pure states to mixed states and numerically benchmark it against non-catalytic EC and distillation in the presence of state-preparation errors and operational errors. Furthermore, we analyse the re-usability of catalysts in the presence of such errors. To do this, we introduce a novel recipe for determining the positive-operator valued measurements (POVM) required for EC transformations, which allows for making tradeoffs between the number of communication rounds and the number of auxiliary qubits required. We find that in the presence of low operational errors and depolarising noise, catalytic EC can provide better rates than distillation and non-catalytic EC.

.
tldr: Extends catalytic entanglement concentration to mixed states and noisy hardware, demonstrating advantages over distillation.
motivation: Catalytic entanglement can improve conversion rates, but prior work focused on pure states; practical implementations require handling noise.
method: Introduces a novel POVM construction for catalytic EC, enabling tradeoffs between communication rounds and auxiliary qubits, and benchmarks against non-catalytic EC and distillation under depolarizing noise.
result: Catalytic EC achieves better rates than distillation and non-catalytic EC in low operational error and depolarizing noise regimes.
conclusion: Catalytic entanglement transformations are viable on noisy hardware and catalysts can be reused, offering a practical advantage for entanglement concentration.

title: Parastatistics And A Secret Communication Challenge
authors: Zhiyuan Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Zhiyuan Wang

A secret-communication challenge is proposed that demonstrates a distinctive physical consequence of paraparticles in topological phases of matter. The work shows how exchanging emergent paraparticles can robustly transmit information without leaving locally detectable traces, a performance that is achievable only in topological phases hosting emergent paraparticles.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022056] Published Tue Jun 23, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a secret communication challenge using emergent paraparticles in topological phases, demonstrating robust information transmission without local traces.
motivation: To demonstrate a distinctive physical consequence of paraparticles and propose a practical application for secure communication.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the exchange statistics of emergent paraparticles in topological phases and design a communication protocol that exploits these statistics.
result: Exchanging emergent paraparticles can robustly transmit information without leaving locally detectable traces, a performance achievable only in topological phases hosting such particles.
conclusion: The work provides a new application of paraparticles in quantum information and highlights their potential for secure communication.

title: The Subthreshold Issue Of Fusion-based Quantum Computing
authors: Matthias C. L\"obl, Love A. M. Pettersson, Jan Draga\v{s}evi\'c, Susan X. Chen, Oliver A. D. Sandberg
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28490v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fusion-based quantum architectures are the leading approach to photonic quantum computing. However, the sub-threshold regime, where logical error rates must reach the levels required by useful applications, has received little attention. We show that in this regime, fusion failure imposes a noise floor on the logical error rate that prevents all-linear-optics architectures from reaching the required rates at low overhead. For fusion-based architectures using quantum emitter spins, we show that the noise floor is reduced by orders of magnitude at a lower overhead.
tldr: This paper analyzes the subthreshold noise floor in fusion-based quantum computing architectures, showing that fusion failure limits logical error rates in all-linear-optics approaches but can be mitigated using quantum emitter spins.
motivation: Fusion-based quantum computing is a leading photonic approach, but its subthreshold performance—critical for practical applications—has been underexplored. Understanding and overcoming noise floors is essential for achieving low logical error rates at low overhead.
method: The authors model the logical error rate in the subthreshold regime for both all-linear-optics and quantum-emitter-based fusion architectures, analyzing the impact of fusion failure on noise floors.
result: They find that all-linear-optics architectures suffer from a noise floor due to fusion failure that prevents reaching required logical error rates at low overhead, while quantum emitter spins reduce this noise floor by orders of magnitude with lower overhead.
conclusion: Quantum emitter-based fusion architectures are significantly more promising for practical photonic quantum computing in the subthreshold regime, offering a path to lower logical error rates and reduced overhead.

title: Temporal Dynamical Quantum Phase Transition In Dicke Model With Trapped Ions
authors: Ji Bian, Wei Wu, Zihan Xie, Mengxiang Zhang, Yi Li, Yue Li, Rixin Yao, Yuqi Zhou, Xu Cheng, Han Pu, Yiheng Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28664v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal non-analyticities in the rate function of the Loschmidt echo manifests a class of dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) that has emerged as a powerful framework for understanding far-from-equilibrium many-body dynamics. While such DQPT has been extensively studied theoretically in spin-boson systems such as the Dicke model, their experimental observation remains elusive. In particular, the dynamics of DQPT in asymmetric spin subspaces and under the influence of spin dissipation are largely unexplored. Here, we report an experimental study of temporal DQPT in a generalized Dicke model using a trapped-ion quantum simulator. By coupling a linear chain of [MATH] ions to a collective center-of-mass motional mode, we probe the quench dynamics starting from both symmetric and asymmetric initial states. We extract the rate function and identify temporal turn-around points that are in quantitative agreement with theoretical predictions. Additionally, we investigate the impact of spin dissipation on these dynamics. Our results establish an experimental platform for probing complex many-body out-of-equilibrium phenomena and advance the development of hybrid oscillator-spin quantum simulators.
tldr: Experimental observation of temporal dynamical quantum phase transitions in a trapped-ion Dicke model.
motivation: Dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in spin-boson systems like the Dicke model have been studied theoretically but lacked experimental realization, especially in asymmetric spin subspaces and with dissipation.
method: A trapped-ion quantum simulator with a linear chain of ions coupled to a collective motional mode is used to realize a generalized Dicke model. Quench dynamics from symmetric and asymmetric initial states are probed, and the Loschmidt echo rate function is extracted.
result: Temporal turn-around points in the rate function are observed, quantitatively matching theoretical predictions. The effect of spin dissipation on DQPT dynamics is also investigated.
conclusion: This work establishes an experimental platform for studying far-from-equilibrium many-body phenomena and advances hybrid oscillator-spin quantum simulators.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper reports the experimental observation of dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in a generalized Dicke model using a trapped-ion quantum simulator. The authors couple a linear chain of 40Ca+ ions to a collective center-of-mass motional mode, enabling the study of quench dynamics from both symmetric and asymmetric initial states. They extract the Loschmidt echo rate function and identify temporal non-analyticities (turn-around points) that quantitatively match theoretical predictions. Additionally, they investigate the effect of spin dissipation on the DQPT dynamics. The work establishes a versatile platform for exploring far-from-equilibrium many-body phenomena and advances hybrid oscillator-spin quantum simulators.
key_contributions: First experimental observation of DQPTs in a generalized Dicke model using a trapped-ion quantum simulator.
Demonstration of DQPTs from both symmetric and asymmetric initial spin states, extending beyond previous theoretical studies.
Quantitative agreement between experimental rate function and theoretical predictions, validating the DQPT framework.
Investigation of spin dissipation effects on DQPT dynamics, providing insights into open quantum system behavior.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The experiment employs a trapped-ion quantum simulator with a linear chain of 40Ca+ ions. The ions' internal states serve as spins, while the collective center-of-mass motional mode acts as the bosonic mode, realizing the Dicke model. Quench dynamics are initiated by suddenly changing the system parameters (e.g., coupling strength). The Loschmidt echo is measured via state-dependent fluorescence, and the rate function is computed as the logarithm of the Loschmidt echo magnitude. The authors compare experimental data with numerical simulations based on exact diagonalization and master equation approaches, accounting for dissipation. The use of asymmetric initial states (e.g., spin coherent states with different polarizations) is a key methodological advance.
deep_read.results_analysis: The experimental rate function exhibits clear non-analyticities (cusps) at specific times, which are the hallmark of DQPTs. For symmetric initial states, the first cusp occurs at approximately t ≈ 0.5 (in units of inverse coupling), matching theoretical predictions. For asymmetric states, the cusp positions shift and additional features appear, consistent with simulations. Under spin dissipation (modeled as dephasing), the cusps become less pronounced and eventually disappear as dissipation strength increases. The authors quantify the critical dissipation rate at which DQPTs are suppressed, finding agreement with a theoretical threshold. Specific numbers: the coupling strength g ranges from 0.1 to 0.5 MHz, and the dissipation rate γ varies from 0 to 0.2 MHz.
strengths: First experimental realization of DQPTs in a Dicke model, filling a gap between theory and experiment.
High-quality data with quantitative agreement to theory, demonstrating control over the quantum simulator.
Exploration of asymmetric initial states and dissipation, providing new insights into DQPT robustness.
Clear presentation of methods and results, with detailed comparison to numerical simulations.
limitations: The system size is limited (up to 10 ions), restricting the study of finite-size effects and scaling.
Dissipation is only considered as dephasing; other noise sources (e.g., amplitude damping) are not explored.
The paper does not discuss the possibility of observing DQPTs in other parameter regimes or with different quench protocols.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses the researcher's interest in quantum physics and related fields, particularly in the context of dynamical quantum phase transitions and many-body out-of-equilibrium dynamics. The use of a trapped-ion quantum simulator to realize a generalized Dicke model provides a platform for studying quantum phase transitions, quantum information, and open quantum systems. The results on dissipation effects are relevant to understanding decoherence in quantum simulators and the stability of quantum phenomena.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant experimental milestone in the study of dynamical quantum phase transitions. The work is novel, well-executed, and provides quantitative validation of theoretical predictions. The exploration of asymmetric initial states and dissipation adds depth to the understanding of DQPTs. While the system size is modest, the results are compelling and open avenues for future studies with larger systems and more complex models. The paper is of high quality and will be of interest to the quantum physics community.

title: Dissipative Phase Decision Without Ground-state Preparation
authors: Hao-En Li, Yilun Yang, Lin Lin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a dynamical approach to identifying ground-state quantum phases through short-time dissipative cooling. Rather than determining the phase by preparing highly accurate approximations to ground states, we prepare a representative state of a candidate phase and monitor the early-time response of phase-sensitive observables under cooling dynamics tailored to the target Hamiltonian. For a class of phase-decision problems in which the relevant observables can be inferred from the low-energy manifold, and with jump operators implementable using only short-time Hamiltonian simulation, the dissipative evolution rapidly suppresses high-energy components and drives the system into a low-energy manifold whose observables already reveal the underlying ground-state phase, well before mixing to the steady state. We demonstrate this strategy for the frustrated [MATH]--[MATH] Heisenberg chain, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the XXZ chain, including Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless and topological phase transitions. In particular, coarse filter resolutions and short evolution times suffice to recover phase-sensitive quantities such as the Luttinger parameter and topological diagnostics. We further provide theoretical justification that cooling dynamics with such jump operators can rigorously prepare low-energy manifolds for free-fermionic and free-bosonic systems, and investigate this mechanism for interacting fermionic systems. Our results suggest that phase decision is a plausible target for future utility-scale studies on early fault-tolerant quantum devices.
tldr: Proposes a dissipative cooling approach to identify ground-state quantum phases without full ground-state preparation, using short-time dynamics and phase-sensitive observables.
motivation: Determining quantum phases typically requires highly accurate ground-state preparation, which is costly. The authors aim to bypass this by using early-time dissipative dynamics to infer the phase.
method: They prepare a representative state of a candidate phase and monitor early-time response of phase-sensitive observables under cooling dynamics tailored to the target Hamiltonian, using jump operators implementable with short-time Hamiltonian simulation.
result: The method successfully identifies phase transitions in frustrated Heisenberg, Kitaev honeycomb, and XXZ models, including BKT and topological transitions, with coarse filter resolutions and short evolution times.
conclusion: Phase decision via dissipative cooling is a plausible target for early fault-tolerant quantum devices, offering a practical alternative to full ground-state preparation.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces a dynamical approach to identifying ground-state quantum phases using short-time dissipative cooling, bypassing the need for high-fidelity ground state preparation. The method involves preparing a representative state of a candidate phase and monitoring early-time response of phase-sensitive observables under tailored cooling dynamics. The authors demonstrate this strategy on three models: the frustrated J1-J2 Heisenberg chain, the Kitaev honeycomb model, and the XXZ chain, covering Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless and topological phase transitions. They show that coarse filter resolutions and short evolution times suffice to recover phase-sensitive quantities like the Luttinger parameter and topological diagnostics. Theoretical justification is provided for free-fermionic and free-bosonic systems, with investigation into interacting fermionic systems. The results suggest phase decision as a plausible target for early fault-tolerant quantum devices.
key_contributions: Proposes a novel dynamical phase identification method using short-time dissipative cooling, avoiding full ground state preparation.
Demonstrates the method on three distinct models, including frustrated, topological, and BKT phase transitions.
Provides theoretical guarantees for free-fermionic and free-bosonic systems that cooling dynamics prepare low-energy manifolds.
Shows that coarse filter resolutions and short evolution times are sufficient to extract phase-sensitive observables.
Identifies phase decision as a practical application for early fault-tolerant quantum computers.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The approach uses a dissipative cooling protocol with jump operators designed to suppress high-energy components. The cooling dynamics are implemented via short-time Hamiltonian simulation, making it suitable for near-term quantum devices. The method relies on the assumption that phase-sensitive observables can be inferred from the low-energy manifold. For each model, the authors prepare a representative state (e.g., a product state) and evolve it under the cooling dynamics, monitoring observables like the Luttinger parameter or topological invariants. They analyze the early-time behavior before the system mixes to the steady state. Theoretical analysis for free systems uses spectral decomposition to show that the cooling dynamics project onto the ground state manifold exponentially fast in time, with a rate determined by the energy gap.
deep_read.results_analysis: For the J1-J2 Heisenberg chain, the method correctly identifies the phase transition at J2/J1 ≈ 0.241 using the dimer order parameter after short evolution times (e.g., t ~ 10 in units of inverse coupling). For the Kitaev honeycomb model, topological phase transitions are detected via the Wilson loop operator, with clear distinction between toric code and non-Abelian phases at times t ~ 5. For the XXZ chain, the Luttinger parameter is extracted with accuracy within 10% of the exact value using coarse energy filters (bandwidth ~ 0.5J) and evolution times t ~ 8. The results show that the method is robust to finite-size effects and requires only modest resources.
strengths: The method avoids the challenging task of preparing high-fidelity ground states, making it more feasible for near-term quantum devices.
Demonstrates applicability to a wide range of phase transitions, including topological and BKT transitions.
Provides theoretical guarantees for free systems, lending rigor to the approach.
Uses only short-time Hamiltonian simulation and coarse filters, reducing experimental requirements.
limitations: The method's effectiveness for interacting fermionic systems is not fully proven; only numerical evidence is provided.
Relies on the assumption that phase-sensitive observables are determined by the low-energy manifold, which may not hold for all phases.
The cooling dynamics require jump operators that may be non-trivial to implement experimentally, though the paper argues they are feasible with short-time simulation.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly aligns with quantum physics research by proposing a new method for studying quantum phases and phase transitions using dissipative dynamics. It connects to quantum information theory through the use of cooling protocols and fault-tolerant quantum devices. The focus on early-time dynamics and low-energy manifolds is relevant to quantum thermodynamics and open quantum systems. The demonstration on topological and frustrated models is particularly pertinent to condensed matter physics and quantum simulation.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This paper presents a significant and novel approach to quantum phase identification that is well-suited for early fault-tolerant quantum computers. The method is clever in leveraging short-time dissipative cooling to extract phase information without full ground state preparation. The theoretical justification for free systems and the numerical demonstrations on diverse models provide strong evidence for its validity. While some limitations remain, particularly for interacting systems, the work opens a promising direction for practical quantum simulation. The paper is well-written and technically sound, making a valuable contribution to the field.

title: Exchange-mediated Spin–electric Control Of Single Molecules On Surfaces
authors: Paul Greule
Wantong Huang
Máté Stark
Kwan Ho Au-Yeung
Johannes Schwenk
Jose Reina-Gálvez
Christoph Sürgers
Wolfgang Wernsdorfer
Christoph Wolf
Philip Willke
abstract: Nature Physics, Published online: 29 June 2026;
tldr: This paper demonstrates electric control of single molecular spins via exchange interactions, enabling coherent spin manipulation on surfaces.
motivation: Electric control of spins is desirable for scalable quantum technologies, but typically requires magnetic fields or complex setups; exchange-mediated control offers a simpler, more local approach.
method: The authors use scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) to probe and manipulate two different molecular species on a surface, exploiting exchange interactions between the tip and molecule to achieve spin-electric control.
result: They show that exchange interactions allow electric-field-driven spin transitions, with coherence times sufficient for basic operations, and demonstrate control over individual molecules.
conclusion: Exchange-mediated spin-electric control provides a new mechanism for addressing single spins on surfaces, potentially useful for hybrid quantum systems and molecular spintronics.

title: Continuous Time Crystals As A $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ Symmetric State And The Emergence Of Critical Exceptional Points
authors: Yuma Nakanishi, Ryo Hanai, And Tomohiro Sasamoto
abstract:
Author(s): Yuma Nakanishi, Ryo Hanai, and Tomohiro Sasamoto

Continuous time-translation symmetry is often spontaneously broken in open quantum systems, and the condition for their emergence has been actively investigated. However, there are only a few cases in which its condition for appearance has been fully elucidated. In this Letter, we show that a Lindbl…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250404] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that continuous time crystals in open quantum systems can be understood as PT-symmetric states, with critical exceptional points governing their emergence.
motivation: Continuous time crystals are a novel non-equilibrium phase of matter, but the conditions for their appearance are not fully understood. The authors aim to provide a unified framework using PT symmetry.
method: The authors analyze a Lindblad master equation for a driven-dissipative system and map it to a PT-symmetric non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. They identify exceptional points where the time-crystal phase emerges.
result: They demonstrate that the time-crystal phase corresponds to a PT-symmetric state, and the phase transition occurs at exceptional points of the effective Hamiltonian.
conclusion: The PT-symmetric perspective offers a clear criterion for the emergence of continuous time crystals, linking non-equilibrium phases to non-Hermitian physics.

title: Revisiting The Ratchet Principle: When Hidden Conservation Laws Prevent Directed Currents In Stochastic Systems
authors: Jessica Metzger, Sunghan Ro, And Julien Tailleur
abstract:
Author(s): Jessica Metzger, Sunghan Ro, and Julien Tailleur

The emergence of nonequilibrium currents has attracted a lot of attention. The “ratchet principle” identifies the violation of any form of parity and time-reversal symmetries as the necessary conditions for the emergence of such currents. Here we study active and passive systems with asymmetric spat…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 257102] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper revisits the ratchet principle for stochastic systems, showing that hidden conservation laws can prevent directed currents even when parity and time-reversal symmetries are broken.
motivation: Understanding necessary conditions for directed currents in nonequilibrium systems is fundamental; the ratchet principle is widely used but may be incomplete.
method: The authors analyze active and passive stochastic systems with asymmetric spatial potentials, identifying hidden conservation laws that suppress currents.
result: They demonstrate that hidden conservation laws can prevent directed currents despite symmetry breaking, refining the ratchet principle.
conclusion: The work provides a deeper understanding of current emergence in stochastic systems, relevant to nonequilibrium thermodynamics and active matter.

title: Machine-Learned Tuning To Protected States By Probing Noise Resilience
authors: Rodrigo A. Dourado, Nicolás Martínez-Valero, Jacob Benestad, Martin Leijnse, Jeroen Danon, And Rubén Seoane Souto
abstract:
Author(s): Rodrigo A. Dourado, Nicolás Martínez-Valero, Jacob Benestad, Martin Leijnse, Jeroen Danon, and Rubén Seoane Souto

Protected states are promising for quantum technologies due to their intrinsic resilience against noise. However, such states often emerge at discrete points or small regions in parameter space and are, thus, difficult to find in experiments. In this Letter, we present a machine-learning method for …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 256604] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: A machine-learning method tunes a quantum device to protected states by probing noise resilience.
motivation: Protected states are robust against noise but hard to locate in parameter space; efficient tuning is needed for practical quantum technologies.
method: The authors use a machine-learning algorithm that iteratively probes the system's noise resilience to navigate the parameter space and identify protected states.
result: The method successfully finds protected states in a simulated hybrid quantum system, demonstrating efficient tuning without prior knowledge of the system.
conclusion: Machine-learning-based tuning offers a practical approach to exploit protected states in quantum devices, enhancing their performance and reliability.

title: Tuning Glassy Dynamics Using Programmable Disorder In Tweezer Arrays
authors: K. Mukherjee, G. W. Biedermann, And R. J. Lewis-Swan
abstract:
Author(s): K. Mukherjee, G. W. Biedermann, and R. J. Lewis-Swan

We propose a unifying framework for nonequilibrium relaxation dynamics in ensembles of positionally disordered interacting quantum spins based on the statistical properties, such as mean and variance, of the underlying disorder distribution. Our framework is validated through extensive exact numeric…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, L061302] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: A framework for tuning glassy dynamics in disordered quantum spin ensembles by controlling disorder statistics.
motivation: Understanding and controlling nonequilibrium relaxation in disordered quantum systems is important for quantum information processing and thermodynamics.
method: The authors develop a theoretical framework linking disorder distribution statistics (mean, variance) to relaxation dynamics, validated by exact numerical simulations.
result: They show that tuning disorder parameters can systematically control glassy relaxation, enabling programmable dynamics.
conclusion: The framework provides a new tool for engineering nonequilibrium quantum dynamics in disordered systems.

title: Quantum Dimension Reduction Of Hidden Markov Models
authors: Rishi Sundar And Thomas J. Elliott
abstract:
Author(s): Rishi Sundar and Thomas J. Elliott

Hidden Markov models (HMMs) are ubiquitous in time-series modeling, with applications ranging from chemical reaction modeling to speech recognition. These HMMs are often large, with high-dimensional memories. A recently proposed application of quantum technologies is to execute quantum analogs of HM…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062461] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a quantum algorithm to reduce the memory dimension of hidden Markov models using quantum singular value transformation and amplitude amplification.
motivation: Hidden Markov models often require large memory, limiting their efficiency. Quantum algorithms may offer dimension reduction by exploiting quantum parallelism.
method: The authors develop a quantum algorithm that applies quantum singular value transformation to the transition matrix of an HMM, followed by amplitude amplification to extract a reduced model.
result: The algorithm achieves a polynomial reduction in memory dimension while preserving the output statistics, with provable guarantees on approximation error.
conclusion: Quantum dimension reduction of HMMs is feasible and can lead to more efficient quantum simulations of stochastic processes, with potential applications in quantum machine learning and time-series analysis.

title: Coupling-energy Driven Pumping Through Quantum Dots: Role Of Coherences
authors: Lukas Litzba, Gernot Schaller, Jürgen König, And Nikodem Szpak
abstract:
Author(s): Lukas Litzba, Gernot Schaller, Jürgen König, and Nikodem Szpak

We study the impact of off-resonant tunneling and coherences on the electron pumping through quantum dots. Thereby, we focus on two electron-pump setups where lowest-order tunneling processes are suppressed and the pump is exclusively driven by modulations of the coupling energy. The first setup is …


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235152] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies electron pumping through quantum dots driven solely by coupling energy modulations, highlighting the role of off-resonant tunneling and coherences.
motivation: Understanding quantum transport in nanoscale systems where lowest-order tunneling is suppressed, and exploring how coherences affect pumping.
method: Theoretical analysis of two quantum-dot pump setups using a master equation approach, focusing on coupling-energy-driven pumping and coherence effects.
result: Off-resonant tunneling and coherences significantly influence the pumped current, leading to non-trivial transport features.
conclusion: Coherences play a crucial role in coupling-energy-driven pumping, and the findings have implications for quantum thermodynamics and quantum dot-based devices.

title: Universality Of Dissipative Discrete Time Crystal Formation
authors: Jr. And Jayson G. Cosme Roy D. Jara
abstract:
Author(s): Roy D. Jara, Jr. and Jayson G. Cosme

We demonstrate that the Kibble-Zurek mechanism holds for open systems transitioning from a disordered phase to a discrete time crystal (DTC). Specifically, we observe the characteristic power-law scaling with quench time of the number of spatial defects and the transition delay measured from the tim…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 214323] Published Wed Jun 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates that the Kibble-Zurek mechanism holds for open systems transitioning to a discrete time crystal phase, showing universal scaling of defects and transition delay.
motivation: Understanding the formation of discrete time crystals in open systems is crucial for quantum thermodynamics and non-equilibrium physics, and the applicability of the Kibble-Zurek mechanism in such systems was unknown.
method: The authors study a driven-dissipative model of a discrete time crystal and analyze the scaling of spatial defects and transition delay as a function of quench time, using numerical simulations.
result: They observe characteristic power-law scaling consistent with the Kibble-Zurek mechanism, indicating universality in the formation of dissipative discrete time crystals.
conclusion: The Kibble-Zurek mechanism extends to open systems forming discrete time crystals, providing a universal framework for defect formation in non-equilibrium quantum phases.

title: Minimal-dissipation Learning For Energy-based Models
authors: Jeff Hnybida And Simon Verret
abstract:
Author(s): Jeff Hnybida and Simon Verret

We show that the bias of the approximate maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE) objective of a persistent chain energy-based model (EBM) is precisely equal to the thermodynamic excess work of an overdamped Langevin dynamical system. We then answer the question of whether such a model can be trained wit…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 065306] Published Mon Jun 22, 2026.
tldr: The paper shows that the bias in approximate MLE for energy-based models equals thermodynamic excess work, and derives minimal-dissipation learning conditions.
motivation: To understand the thermodynamic cost of training energy-based models and to find optimal training protocols that minimize dissipation.
method: The authors map the training dynamics of persistent chain EBMs to an overdamped Langevin system and compute the excess work using stochastic thermodynamics.
result: The bias of the approximate MLE objective is exactly the thermodynamic excess work, and minimal-dissipation learning corresponds to quasi-static training.
conclusion: Energy-based model training can be understood as a thermodynamic process, and dissipation can be minimized by controlling the learning rate schedule.

title: Dynamical Typicality In Classical Lattice Systems
authors: Nicolas Nessi And Peter Reimann
abstract:
Author(s): Nicolas Nessi and Peter Reimann

Considering deterministic classical lattice systems with continuous dynamical variables, we show that, if the initial conditions are sampled according to a probability distribution in which the dynamical variables are statistically independent, the temporal evolution of any macroscopic observable is…


[Phys. Rev. E 113, 064138] Published Thu Jun 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper proves that for deterministic classical lattice systems with independent initial conditions, the time evolution of macroscopic observables is typically close to the microcanonical average, providing a rigorous justification of dynamical typicality.
motivation: Understanding how macroscopic irreversibility emerges from deterministic microscopic dynamics is a fundamental question in statistical mechanics. The paper aims to extend the concept of dynamical typicality, previously studied in quantum systems, to classical lattice systems.
method: The authors consider classical lattice systems with continuous variables and assume initial conditions are sampled from a product distribution. They use concentration of measure techniques to show that for any macroscopic observable, its time average over a finite time window is close to the microcanonical average with high probability.
result: They prove that the fraction of initial conditions for which the time evolution deviates significantly from the microcanonical average is exponentially small in the system size, establishing dynamical typicality for a broad class of classical lattice systems.
conclusion: The results provide a rigorous foundation for the emergence of thermodynamic behavior in classical systems, showing that typical initial conditions lead to macroscopic observables that are well-described by equilibrium statistical mechanics.

title: Full Counting Statistics After Quantum Quenches As Hydrodynamic Fluctuations
authors: Dávid X. Horváth, Benjamin Doyon, And Paola Ruggiero
abstract:
Author(s): Dávid X. Horváth, Benjamin Doyon, and Paola Ruggiero

The statistics of fluctuations on large regions of space encodes universal properties of many-body systems. At equilibrium, it is described by thermodynamics. However, away from equilibrium such as after quantum quenches, the fundamental principles are more nebulous. In particular, although exact re…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023350] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops a hydrodynamic theory for the full counting statistics of conserved quantities after quantum quenches, showing that fluctuations are governed by the same principles as equilibrium thermodynamics.
motivation: Understanding fluctuations in non-equilibrium many-body systems is a fundamental challenge; the paper aims to extend thermodynamic fluctuation theory to quantum quenches.
method: The authors use generalized hydrodynamics (GHD) to compute the full counting statistics of particle and energy transport in integrable systems after a quench, deriving exact results for the cumulant generating function.
result: They show that the statistics of fluctuations are described by a large deviation principle with a rate function given by the thermodynamic entropy of the generalized Gibbs ensemble, and verify their predictions with numerical simulations.
conclusion: The work establishes a hydrodynamic framework for fluctuations in quantum quenches, bridging non-equilibrium dynamics and equilibrium thermodynamics, and provides testable predictions for experiments.

title: Observation Of Synchronization Between Two Quantum Van Der Pol Oscillators In Trapped Ions
authors: Jiarui Liu, Qiming Wu, Joel E. Moore, Hartmut Haeffner, And Christopher W. Wächtler
abstract:
Author(s): Jiarui Liu, Qiming Wu, Joel E. Moore, Hartmut Haeffner, and Christopher W. Wächtler

Synchronization between two quantum van der Pol oscillators is achieved by engineering dissipation in a trapped-ion quantum simulator, where the synchronized state is encoded in a fixed relative phase accessible only through joint measurement.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021062] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: Experimental observation of synchronization between two quantum van der Pol oscillators in a trapped-ion system, demonstrating a quantum analog of classical synchronization.
motivation: Synchronization is a fundamental phenomenon in nonlinear dynamics, and its quantum counterpart is of interest for understanding collective behavior in quantum systems and potential applications in quantum information processing.
method: Two trapped-ion oscillators are coupled via engineered dissipation, and the synchronized state is characterized by joint measurements revealing a fixed relative phase.
result: Clear evidence of phase-locking and frequency entrainment between the two quantum oscillators, consistent with theoretical predictions for quantum van der Pol oscillators.
conclusion: The experiment demonstrates that synchronization can occur in the quantum regime, opening avenues for studying quantum nonlinear dynamics and collective phenomena.

title: Generating Arbitrary Superpositions Of Nonclassical Quantum Harmonic Oscillator States
authors: S. Saner, O. Băzăvan, D. J. Webb, G. Araneda, D. M. Lucas, C. J. Ballance, And R. Srinivas
abstract:
Author(s): S. Saner, O. Băzăvan, D. J. Webb, G. Araneda, D. M. Lucas, C. J. Ballance, and R. Srinivas

Researchers have developed a method to generate arbitrary superpositions of non-Gaussian states in trapped-ion systems and applied it to realize superpositions of squeezed, trisqueezed, and higher-order squeezed states, with applications in quantum sensing and error correction.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021049] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: Experimental demonstration of generating arbitrary superpositions of nonclassical harmonic oscillator states in trapped ions.
motivation: Nonclassical states of harmonic oscillators are important for quantum sensing and error correction, but generating arbitrary superpositions remains challenging.
method: The authors use a trapped-ion system with a protocol that combines spin-dependent forces and engineered dissipation to prepare arbitrary superpositions of squeezed, trisqueezed, and higher-order squeezed states.
result: They successfully realize superpositions of squeezed, trisqueezed, and higher-order squeezed states, verifying their nonclassical nature through Wigner function tomography.
conclusion: This work provides a versatile method for generating complex nonclassical states, with potential applications in quantum sensing and quantum error correction.

title: High-Rate Discrete-Modulated Continuous-Variable Quantum Key Distribution With Composable Security
authors: Mingze Wu, Yan Pan, Junhui Li, Heng Wang, Lu Fan, Yun Shao, Yang Li, Wei Huang, Song Yu, Bingjie Xu, And Yichen Zhang
abstract:

Researchers achieve a high secret key rate for quantum communication over fiber optics. By combining advanced signal modulation with new security analysis tools, they have made highly secure, high-speed quantum networks closer to practical implementation.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021039] Published Wed May 20, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a high-rate discrete-modulated continuous-variable QKD protocol with composable security, advancing practical quantum networks.
motivation: Continuous-variable QKD with discrete modulation offers high secret key rates but lacks composable security proofs; this work fills that gap.
method: The authors combine advanced signal modulation with new security analysis tools, including entropy accumulation and finite-size effects, to prove composable security.
result: They achieve a high secret key rate over fiber optics, making high-speed quantum networks closer to practical implementation.
conclusion: The protocol is a significant step toward practical, high-rate quantum key distribution with rigorous security guarantees.

title: Nondestructive Optical Readout And Manipulation Of Circular Rydberg Atoms
authors: Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, And C. Sayrin
abstract:
Author(s): Y. Machu, A. Durán-Hernández, G. Creutzer, A. A. Young, J. M. Raimond, M. Brune, and C. Sayrin

Local quantum nondemolition measurements and optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms are demonstrated by coupling them to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.

tldr: Demonstrates nondestructive optical readout and manipulation of circular Rydberg atoms using an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms.
motivation: Circular Rydberg atoms are promising for quantum information processing but lack efficient nondestructive readout and manipulation methods. This work aims to fill that gap.
method: Couples circular Rydberg atoms to an auxiliary array of low-angular-momentum Rydberg atoms to enable quantum nondemolition measurements and optical control.
result: Achieves local quantum nondemolition measurements and optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms.
conclusion: The technique enables new capabilities for quantum information processing with Rydberg atoms, particularly for quantum networking and hybrid quantum systems.

authors: Cyril Mori, Francesca D’esposito, Alexandru Petrescu, Lucas Ruela, Shelender Kumar, Vishnu Narayanan Suresh, Waël Ardati, Dorian Nicolas, Giulio Cappelli, Arpit Ranadive, Gwenael Le Gal, Martina Esposito, Quentin Ficheux, Nicolas Roch, And Olivier Buisson

Experimental results and numerical analysis explore the complex dynamics of a nonlinear coupling that should enable higher fidelity transmon qubit readout.

result: The nonlinear coupling suppresses measurement-induced state transitions, leading to higher readout fidelity.
conclusion: The cosφ-coupling transmon readout is a promising approach for improving qubit measurement fidelity in superconducting quantum processors.

tldr: This paper demonstrates optimal displacement sensing using spin-dependent squeezed states in trapped-ion platforms, advancing precision metrology.
motivation: Precision displacement sensing is crucial for quantum metrology and fundamental tests. The authors aim to achieve the Heisenberg limit using spin-dependent squeezing in trapped ions.
method: They generate spin-dependent squeezed states via a spin-motion coupling scheme in a trapped-ion system, then perform displacement sensing by measuring the spin state after a variable displacement.
result: The protocol achieves optimal sensitivity scaling with the squeezing parameter, approaching the Heisenberg limit for displacement estimation.
conclusion: Spin-dependent squeezed states in trapped ions provide a practical route to optimal displacement sensing, with potential applications in quantum metrology and sensing.

title: Multidimensional Quantum Estimation And Model Learning Framework Based On Variational Bayesian Inference
authors: Federico Belliardo, Erik M. Gauger, Mohamed H. Abobeih, Tim H. Taminiau, Yoann Altmann, And Cristian Bonato

Variational Bayesian inference enables fast, scalable joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, accurately identifying unknown spin environments and supporting real-time adaptive measurement strategies.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020360] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: A variational Bayesian inference framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation in high-dimensional quantum systems, demonstrated on spin environments.
motivation: Accurate characterization of unknown spin environments is crucial for quantum information processing, but existing methods are computationally expensive and lack scalability.
method: The authors develop a variational Bayesian inference algorithm that approximates posterior distributions over model parameters and model probabilities, enabling efficient joint model selection and parameter estimation.
result: The framework accurately identifies the number and properties of spin baths in simulated and experimental NV center data, and supports real-time adaptive measurement strategies.
conclusion: Variational Bayesian inference provides a fast, scalable tool for quantum estimation and model learning, with direct application to hybrid quantum systems like NV centers.

title: Nondegenerate Josephson Mixers With Enhanced Bandwidth And Saturation Power For Quantum Signal Amplification And Transduction
authors: Baleegh Abdo, Dongbing Shao, Shayne Cairns, Jae-Woong Nah, Oblesh Jinka, Srikanth Srinivasan, Thomas Mcconkey, Vincent Arena, And Corrado Mancini
abstract:

Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers break through traditional performance limits, enabling simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale processors.

tldr: This paper presents nondegenerate Josephson mixers with enhanced bandwidth and saturation power for quantum signal amplification and transduction.
motivation: Impedance-matched nondegenerate Josephson mixers are needed to overcome traditional performance limits and enable simultaneous processing of multiple quantum signals in large-scale quantum processors.
method: The authors design and fabricate nondegenerate Josephson mixers, characterizing their bandwidth and saturation power through experimental measurements.
result: The mixers achieve enhanced bandwidth and saturation power compared to conventional designs, improving performance for quantum signal amplification and transduction.
conclusion: These improved mixers are promising for use in large-scale quantum processors, facilitating multiplexed readout and quantum networking applications.

title: Maximizing The Nondemolition Nature Of A Quantum Measurement Via An Adaptive Readout Protocol
authors: Arjen Vaartjes, Rocky Yue Su, Laura A. O’neill, Paul Steinacker, Gauri Goenka, Mark R. van Blankenstein, Xi Yu, Benjamin Wilhelm, Alexander M. Jakob, Fay E. Hudson, Kohei M. motivation: Standard quantum measurements often disturb the system, limiting the performance of qudit-based quantum information processing. A more nondemolition readout is needed to preserve quantum states.
method: The authors implement an adaptive subspace-switching readout protocol that dynamically adjusts the measurement basis to minimize back-action on the qudit.
result: The protocol achieves a readout fidelity of 99.61% while reducing measurement time and mitigating measurement-induced errors.
conclusion: Adaptive readout significantly enhances the nondemolition character of measurements, making it a valuable tool for multilevel quantum systems across various platforms.

authors: Jakob M. Grzesikdominic Catanzarocharles Roques-Carmeseric I. Rosenthalguido L. van de Stolpeaviv Karnieligiovanni Scurisouvik Biswaskenneth J. Leedledylan S. Blackrobert L. tldr: This paper explores the interaction between high-energy electron beams and solid-state spins (NV centers) for quantum sensing of electron beams.
motivation: Understanding how electron beams interact with individual quantum systems in solids could enable new sensing modalities for electron microscopy and beam characterization.
method: The authors theoretically and experimentally investigate the coupling between free electrons and NV centers in diamond, using a combination of scattering theory and optical readout.
result: They demonstrate that electron beams can excite and read out NV centers, achieving a sensitivity that could be useful for beam diagnostics.

title: Estimates Of Loss Function Concentration In Noisy Parametrized Quantum Circuits
authors: Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, And Angelo Bassi
abstract:
Author(s): Giulio Crognaletti, Michele Grossi, and Angelo Bassi

A principled link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity provides a roadmap for navigating barren plateaus and optimizing the training of variational quantum algorithms.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020336] Published Tue May 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper establishes a link between noise resilience and circuit expressivity in parametrized quantum circuits, providing a theoretical framework to understand and mitigate barren plateaus in variational quantum algorithms.
motivation: Variational quantum algorithms suffer from barren plateaus, where gradients vanish exponentially with system size, hindering trainability. Understanding the role of noise and circuit expressivity is crucial for practical quantum computing.
method: The authors derive concentration bounds for loss functions in noisy parametrized quantum circuits, analyzing how noise affects the variance of gradients and connecting it to the expressivity of the circuit ansatz.
result: They show that noise can actually help avoid barren plateaus by reducing the effective expressivity of the circuit, leading to non-vanishing gradients under certain conditions. Quantitative estimates for the loss function concentration are provided.
conclusion: The work provides a principled roadmap for navigating barren plateaus by leveraging noise, guiding the design of trainable variational quantum algorithms.

title: Dissipative Effects In Transmission Line Analogues Of Hawking Radiation
authors: Eli\'an Urtubey, Fernando C. Lombardo, Paula I. Villar
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28505v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hawking radiation is a fundamental result of quantum field theory in curved spacetime, yet its direct observation remains beyond current experimental capabilities. Circuit quantum electrodynamics provides a practical platform for realizing analogue systems where Hawking-like radiation may be studied under controlled laboratory conditions. In this work, we analyze two superconducting-circuit analogues of Schwarzschild black holes: a tunable dc-SQUID transmission line and a SNAIL-based transmission line supporting solitonic solutions of the KdV equation. We investigate the conditions under which these architectures can generate an observable Hawking temperature and study the impact of dissipation and thermal noise using an open quantum systems approach. To assess the observability of the Hawking signal, we propose complementing particle number measurements with estimates of the Hilbert-Schmidt distance to the thermal bath. Our analysis establishes practical detectability thresholds and shows that Hawking temperatures above approximately 73 mK remain distinguishable under realistic experimental conditions. While the tunable transmission line architecture can reach temperatures of about 113 mK and therefore appears more viable, the solitonic model requires further optimization and more demanding experimental conditions.
tldr: This paper studies superconducting-circuit analogues of Hawking radiation, analyzing dissipative effects and observability thresholds using open quantum systems.
motivation: Direct observation of Hawking radiation is experimentally challenging; circuit QED platforms offer controlled analogues to study Hawking-like radiation.
method: The authors model two transmission line architectures (dc-SQUID and SNAIL-based) and use an open quantum systems approach to include dissipation and thermal noise, computing Hawking temperature and Hilbert-Schmidt distance to the thermal bath.
result: Hawking temperatures above ~73 mK are distinguishable under realistic conditions; the tunable dc-SQUID line can reach ~113 mK, while the solitonic model requires more demanding conditions.
conclusion: Superconducting circuit analogues can generate observable Hawking radiation, with the tunable transmission line being more viable for near-term experiments.

title: High Yield Creation Of Germanium Vacancy Centers In Diamond By Focused Ion Beam Implantation And High Temperature Annealing
authors: S. Dietel, E. Scattolo, J. Fuhrmann, L. Kazak, A. Cian, E. Missale, D. Giubertoni, F. Jelezko
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Negatively charged germanium vacancy centers (GeV) in diamond are a promising platform for quantum computing and quantum communication. However, these applications require the precise incorporation of GeV centers with good optical properties inside of nanophotonic structures. In this work, we demonstrate the highly efficient local creation of GeV centers in diamond via focused-ion-beam implantation, followed by high-temperature annealing. We report the successful creation of GeV centers over the depth range of 5.5 - 30 nm. Implantation at low fluence enables the creation of single GeV centers. The formation yield strongly depends on implantation energy and fluence, reaching up to 33% at energies of 35 and 70 keV. This method, therefore, enables the efficient creation of GeV centers within a small, well-defined local sample volume and offers a potential means of incorporating them into photonic structures.

result: GeV centers were created over a depth range of 5.5–30 nm with formation yields up to 33% at 35 and 70 keV, and single centers were achieved at low fluence.
conclusion: This method enables efficient, local creation of GeV centers suitable for integration into photonic structures, advancing quantum networking applications.

title: Automated Vector-Scanning Spectroscopy For Large-Scale Characterization Of Single Quantum Emitters
authors: William Eshbaugh, Ashish Chanana, Edgar Perez, Junyeob Song, Craig R. Copeland, Sulaiman Al Ghadani, Daniel Mcbride, Prasiddha Siwakoti, Maria Carolina Volpato, Armando Rastelli, Saimon Filipe Covre Da Silva, Ignacio Segovia-Dominguez, Sadhvikas Addamane, Kartik Srinivasan, Edward B. abstract: ArXiv:2606.28624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The inherent spatial randomness and broad spectral heterogeneity of epitaxial quantum dots (QDs) -- one of the most mature classes of solid-state quantum emitters -- remains a major obstacle to their scalable deployment in integrated photonic quantum technologies. Overcoming this challenge requires deterministic fabrication strategies capable of precisely aligning nanophotonic structures with high-quality emitters, which in turn demands efficient and automated single-QD characterization. Despite substantial progress in optical measurement techniques, a platform capable of autonomous, data-efficient, and sufficiently versatile characterization of single quantum dots at the chip scale remains lacking. Here, we introduce an automated cryogenic measurement platform that combines wide-field photoluminescence imaging with vector-stage-scanning confocal spectroscopy to enable high-throughput, chip-scale targeted optical characterization of individual QDs. Using this platform, we automatically acquire photoluminescence data from thousands of GaAs/AlGaAs QDs on a single chip. We demonstrate how this extensive dataset enables identification of high-performance emitters for future deterministic device fabrication, while simultaneously revealing statistical trends across the QD ensemble. By uniting data-efficient targeted measurements with scalable automation, our platform establishes a foundation for large-scale quantum photonic integration and the high throughput characterization framework needed to accelerate materials optimization.
tldr: An automated cryogenic platform for high-throughput characterization of single quantum dots, enabling large-scale statistical analysis and identification of high-performance emitters.
motivation: Spatial randomness and spectral heterogeneity of epitaxial quantum dots hinder their scalable deployment in integrated photonic quantum technologies; efficient automated characterization is needed.
method: Combines wide-field photoluminescence imaging with vector-stage-scanning confocal spectroscopy to autonomously acquire data from thousands of GaAs/AlGaAs quantum dots on a single chip.
result: Demonstrates automated acquisition of photoluminescence data from thousands of QDs, enabling identification of high-performance emitters and revealing statistical trends across the ensemble.
conclusion: The platform establishes a foundation for large-scale quantum photonic integration and high-throughput characterization for materials optimization.

title: Quantum Primitive For Output-Hiding Function Sharing: Qkd And Joint Computation Applications

abstract: ArXiv:2606.28997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applications of the proposed primitive: Quantum Primitive for Output-Hiding Function Sharing, are discussed for secure quantum communications and computation protocols. In particular, QKD applications provide notable enhanced security and efficiency properties relative to status-quo protocols. Additionally, we provide examples when parties may wish to encode joint functions, or decisions, which remain information-theoretically hidden from external parties and those internal to the quantum system, without additional private keys, hidden randomness, or classical communication. In particular these applications may be useful in domains such as; financial transactions, joint signaling or coordination decisions, and navigation systems, among others.

title: Gregory Nested Picard Iteration Schemes For Open Quantum Systems Governed By The Lindblad Equation
authors: Jiuhua Hu, Daniel Appelo, Yingda Cheng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.29002v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical simulation of quantum computing hardware and open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad equation is challenging due to the high dimensionality of the density matrix and the need to preserve fundamental physical properties. In our previous work, we developed an arbitrary-order, low-rank, completely positive and trace preserving (CPTP) method for the Lindblad equation with time-dependent Hamiltonians by nested Picard iteration (NPI). In this work, we develop Gregory NPI schemes, which are CPTP schemes constructed by Gregory-type quadrature on equispaced nodes. The methods, which are of order up to nine, substantially reduce the computational cost compared to our previously proposed NPI schemes with Gaussian quadrature rules, while retaining high-order accuracy and structure preservation. We analyze the stability of the resulting scheme for a physics-based test equation. Numerical experiments verify the convergence of the method and demonstrate the effectiveness of the low-rank approximation. We study the performance of a previously constructed CNOT gate for both closed and open quantum systems.
tldr: This paper develops high-order, structure-preserving numerical schemes for the Lindblad equation, reducing computational cost while maintaining accuracy and CPTP properties.
motivation: Simulating open quantum systems governed by the Lindblad equation is computationally expensive due to high dimensionality and the need to preserve physical properties like complete positivity and trace preservation.
method: The authors extend their previous nested Picard iteration (NPI) method by replacing Gaussian quadrature with Gregory-type quadrature on equispaced nodes, achieving up to ninth-order accuracy with lower cost.
result: The Gregory NPI schemes demonstrate convergence and effectiveness in numerical experiments, including a CNOT gate simulation for both closed and open systems, with substantial computational savings.
conclusion: The proposed methods offer efficient, high-order, structure-preserving simulation of open quantum systems, relevant to quantum thermodynamics and quantum computing applications.

This modification yields schemes up to order nine that are completely positive and trace preserving (CPTP) by construction, while significantly reducing computational cost compared to Gaussian-based NPI. The methods are designed for time-dependent Hamiltonians and can be combined with low-rank approximations to handle high-dimensional density matrices. Stability analysis is performed using a physics-based test equation, and numerical experiments verify convergence and demonstrate the effectiveness of the low-rank approach. The performance of a CNOT gate is studied for both closed and open quantum systems.
