title: Quantum Fourier Generative Models Trainable At Large Scale
authors: Cenk T\"uys\"uz, Oleksandr Kyriienko, Michele Grossi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28483v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose an algorithmic framework for building and training quantum generative models corresponding to multivariate probability distributions. Our model uses parallel Fourier feature maps for embedding continuous-valued variables combined with a forrelation-type quantum circuit for tuning Fourier coefficients of the quantum model. Crucially, we develop a distinct training strategy where training is enabled at large scale by log-likelihood loss with unbiased Monte Carlo estimator based on Parseval's identity. Unlike prior work that relied on maximal mean discrepancy (MMD) loss, our approach goes beyond matching just low frequency moments, while enabling efficient classical training. Once the model is trained, we use inverse quantum Fourier transforms to map it into a separate sampling circuit in the computational basis. We demonstrate the efficiency of the suggested framework by validating loss estimation at the scale of over 1000 qubits on a single GPU. We show that univariate and bivariate models with highly non-trivial structure can be trained to low total variation distance, while fine-tuned IQP models with MMD loss show poor performance. Comparing to classical baselines represented by normalizing flow and diffusion models, we show that our approach avoids oversmoothing and preserves multi-modal structure of the target. Finally, we have deployed the trained models on superconducting quantum devices, successfully sampling distributions with per-sample execution times of approximately [MATH]. Our work shows that quantum generative models with the train-on-classical deploy-on-quantum approach can provide both high-quality structure at increased scale and fast sampling access needed for inference.
tldr: Proposes a quantum generative model using Fourier feature maps and forrelation circuits, trained via log-likelihood with Monte Carlo estimation, enabling large-scale classical training and quantum sampling.
motivation: Existing quantum generative models rely on MMD loss which only matches low-frequency moments and cannot scale. The authors aim to train high-quality quantum generative models at large scale using a train-on-classical deploy-on-quantum approach.

Training uses log-likelihood loss with an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator based on Parseval's identity, enabling efficient classical training. After training, inverse QFT maps the model to a sampling circuit.
result: Demonstrates loss estimation at over 1000 qubits on a single GPU. Univariate and bivariate models achieve low total variation distance, outperforming IQP models with MMD loss. Compared to normalizing flows and diffusion models, the approach avoids oversmoothing and preserves multi-modal structure. Deployed on superconducting quantum devices with fast sampling.
conclusion: The proposed framework enables high-quality quantum generative models at increased scale with fast sampling, showing promise for practical quantum advantage in generative modeling.

The authors demonstrate that univariate and bivariate models with complex structures can be trained to low total variation distance, outperforming fine-tuned IQP models with MMD loss. title: Enhancing Initial-State Sensitivity Through Time-Dependent Hamiltonian Readout In Ising Spin Chains
authors: Hoang van Do
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local observables can lose sensitivity to an initial state during strongly interacting many-body evolution even though the global dynamics remain unitary. We show that this sensitivity can be enhanced through a time-dependent Hamiltonian readout. Two orthogonal product states are first evolved under a slanted-field Ising Hamiltonian, where their distinction becomes strongly suppressed as observed through several local observables, including subsystem magnetizations and correlation functions, and are then quenched to the transverse-field Ising model at a tunable time. Exact simulations of chains up to [MATH] show that the optimized time-averaged separation after the switch exceeds the residual slanted-field baseline for every observable and system size tested. In the strongest channels, the standardized readout separation remains robust over the accessible size range, with no clear systematic suppression at larger [MATH]. The enhancement recurs in widely separated late-time windows and persists qualitatively for open boundaries. These results establish Hamiltonian switching as an observable-selective mechanism for enhancing initial-state sensitivity without time reversal or implying recovery of the full reduced state.
tldr: This paper shows that switching the Hamiltonian during evolution can enhance the distinguishability of initially orthogonal states in an Ising spin chain, without time reversal.
motivation: Local observables often lose sensitivity to initial states in many-body dynamics; the authors seek a method to recover or enhance this sensitivity without full state tomography.
method: Two orthogonal product states evolve under a slanted-field Ising Hamiltonian, then are quenched to the transverse-field Ising model at a tunable time; exact simulations for chains up to N=12 are performed.
result: The optimized time-averaged separation after the switch exceeds the residual slanted-field baseline for all observables and system sizes tested, and the enhancement persists in late-time windows.
conclusion: Hamiltonian switching provides an observable-selective mechanism to enhance initial-state sensitivity without time reversal, though it does not recover the full reduced state.

title: Quantum Primitive For Output-Hiding Function Sharing: Strategic Settings

abstract: ArXiv:2606.29007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Applications of the proposed primitive: Quantum Primitive for Output-Hiding Function Sharing are discussed for environments in which the parties may have strategic considerations over the generated function value, and therefore may not be mutually trusted. We show that in environments in which the measurement may not be reliably controlled by either party, the primitive permits the parties to generate private, unbiased coins.

title: Quantifying Quantum Correlations In Annihilation Photon Pairs Under Compton Scattering
authors: Z. Riazi Z. Askaripour Ravari
abstract: ArXiv:2606.29035v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a theoretical study of the evolution of polarization entanglement and quantum coherence in 511 keV photon pairs produced by para-positronium decay during successive Compton scattering events. We start with a maximally entangled Bell state and employ the generalized Stokes-Mueller formalism to derive the two-photon density matrix following single-, double-, and triple-Compton scattering, explicitly considering both polar and azimuthal scattering geometries. Using this framework, we quantify the degradation of quantum correlations through concurrence (as a measure of entanglement) and the [MATH]-norm (as a measure of coherence). Our results demonstrate that entanglement is highly sensitive to the scattering geometry and disappears near right-angle scattering, while quantum coherence remains finite even in regimes where entanglement vanishes completely. These findings provide a unified description of polarization-dependent decoherence in annihilation photon pairs and clarify the distinct roles of entanglement and coherence in realistic two-photon interactions. These results are relevant for quantum-enhanced positron emission tomography and highlight the persistence of quantum resources in scattering-dominated media.
tldr: This paper studies the degradation of polarization entanglement and coherence in 511 keV photon pairs from positronium decay under Compton scattering.
motivation: Understanding how quantum correlations degrade in scattering media is relevant for quantum-enhanced positron emission tomography and fundamental tests of quantum mechanics.
method: The authors use the generalized Stokes-Mueller formalism to derive the two-photon density matrix after single, double, and triple Compton scattering, and quantify entanglement via concurrence and coherence via l1-norm.
result: Entanglement is highly sensitive to scattering geometry and vanishes near right-angle scattering, while coherence remains finite even when entanglement is zero.
conclusion: The work provides a unified description of polarization-dependent decoherence in annihilation photon pairs, highlighting the persistence of quantum resources in scattering-dominated media.

method: The authors numerically simulate the mixed-field quantum Ising model on Erdős–Rényi graphs and compute spectral statistics, out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs), and other chaos indicators as a function of graph connectivity.

conclusion: The work provides insights into quantum chaos on random graphs but does not directly address thermodynamic bounds, information processing, or quantum speed limits, making it only tangentially relevant to information thermodynamics.

motivation: To realize a robust platform for simulating chiral quantum magnetism, which is relevant to quantum information and condensed matter physics.

result: The system exhibits a Luttinger liquid phase, demonstrating the feasibility of simulating chiral quantum magnetism with molecular arrays.

title: Intrinsic Nonreciprocity In Electron-phonon-interaction-driven Thermoelectric Diodes
authors: Hao-Kun Ke, Lie-Run Tian, Jun-Feng Liu, Pei-Hao Fu, Jun Wang, And Hu Xu
abstract:

Researchers demonstrate intrinsic nonreciprocal thermoelectric transport in electron-phonon coupled nanowire devices, arising from asymmetric phonon emission and absorption and structural asymmetry. The intrinsic nonreciprocity results in a load-resistor resistance reduction effect that violates Ohm’s addition law in the incoherent limit.


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, L022058] Published Thu Jun 25, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates intrinsic nonreciprocal thermoelectric transport in electron-phonon coupled nanowire devices, leading to a violation of Ohm's addition law.
motivation: Understanding and controlling nonreciprocal transport in thermoelectric devices is important for energy conversion and thermal management.
method: The authors study electron-phonon coupled nanowire devices with structural asymmetry, analyzing phonon emission and absorption processes.
result: They observe intrinsic nonreciprocity that results in a load-resistor resistance reduction effect violating Ohm's addition law in the incoherent limit.
conclusion: The work reveals a new mechanism for nonreciprocal thermoelectric transport, which could be exploited for novel device applications.

title: Rotation Sensor Based On An Atom-cavity System

tldr: Proposes an atom-cavity system as a rotation sensor with sensitivity scaling with the area enclosed by the atomic array.
motivation: To develop a rotation sensor that leverages quantum systems for enhanced sensitivity, potentially useful for inertial navigation or fundamental physics.
method: Uses a transversely pumped atom-cavity system operating near a critical transition; cavity-emitted light probes changes in rotation frequency.
result: The sensor's sensitivity scales with the area enclosed by the atomic array, indicating a quantum advantage in rotation sensing.
conclusion: The atom-cavity system offers a promising platform for rotation sensing, though further development is needed for practical applications.

title: Beyond Stellar Rank: Control Parameters For Scalable Optical Non-Gaussian State Generation

motivation: Non-Gaussian quantum states are essential for quantum information processing, but their generation is inefficient; the authors aim to improve scalability.
method: They propose and experimentally demonstrate control parameters beyond the stellar rank to systematically optimize the generation of non-Gaussian states.
result: The new parameters enable orders-of-magnitude improvement in success probability for generating states like cat states and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill states.
conclusion: This work provides a practical framework for scalable non-Gaussian state generation, advancing optical quantum computing and quantum information applications.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This perspective explores how biomolecular condensation in living cells can be viewed as a computational framework that processes high-dimensional environmental information, potentially using phase transitions.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals to respond appropriately; the authors propose that phase-separated condensates could serve as a substrate for information processing.
method: The paper is a perspective that draws analogies between phase transitions in soft matter and computational primitives, discussing how condensates can sense, classify, and respond to signals.
result: The authors argue that condensates can implement high-dimensional sensing and classification, and that phase transitions enable nonlinear responses and memory.
conclusion: Biomolecular condensation offers a powerful framework for cellular computation, but the connection to information thermodynamics is conceptual rather than quantitative.

tldr: This paper characterizes the quantum computational complexity of matrix functions, identifying regimes where quantum advantage may exist.
motivation: Understanding the complexity of matrix functions is fundamental to quantum computing, but the paper focuses on computational complexity rather than information-theoretic aspects.
method: The authors analyze different parameter regimes of matrix function problems using complexity theory, likely employing reductions and oracle separations.
result: They provide a characterization of the complexity landscape, showing where quantum algorithms can outperform classical ones.
conclusion: The work offers insights into potential quantum advantage for matrix function problems, but it is more aligned with quantum complexity theory than the researcher's core interests.

title: Symmetry-Accelerated Classical Simulation Of Clifford-Dominated Circuits

Author(s): Giulio Camillo, Filipa C.R. Peres, Markus Heinrich, and Juani Bermejo-Vega

tldr: This paper uses symmetry reduction to accelerate classical simulation of Clifford-dominated circuits by optimizing stabilizer decompositions.
motivation: Classical simulation of quantum circuits is important for verification and benchmarking, but stabilizer-based methods become costly for circuits with many non-Clifford gates.
method: The authors exploit strong and weak symmetries of the circuit to reduce the number of terms in the stabilizer decomposition, making the simulation tractable for larger systems.
result: They demonstrate that symmetry-accelerated decompositions can handle multiqubit unitaries beyond previous limits, reducing computational overhead.
conclusion: Symmetry reduction is an effective technique for improving classical simulation of near-Clifford circuits, relevant for quantum advantage experiments.

title: Efficient Simulation Of Logical Magic State Preparation Protocols

abstract:

method: The method propagates errors through the circuit to the end, reducing the complexity of simulating logical magic state preparation protocols.
result: The approach enables efficient classical simulation of a large class of logical magic state preparation protocols.

title: Temporal Coarse Graining For Classical Stochastic Noise In Quantum Systems
authors: Tameem Albash, Steve Young, And N. Tobias Jacobson
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2137 (2026).

Simulations of quantum systems with Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise can be challenging when the noise exhibits temporal correlations over a multitude of time scales, such as for [MATH] noise in solid-state quantum information processors. Here we present an approach for simulating Hamiltonian classical stochastic noise that performs temporal coarse-graining by effectively integrating out the high-frequency components of the noise. We focus on the case where the stochastic noise can be expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes. Temporal coarse-graining is then achieved by conditioning the stochastic process on a coarse realization of the noise, expressing the conditioned stochastic process in terms of a sum of smooth, deterministic functions and bridge processes with boundaries fixed at zero, and performing the ensemble average over the bridge processes. For Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, the deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the stochastic bridge processes are not only independent but taken from the same distribution with correlators that can be expressed analytically, allowing the associated noise propagators to be precomputed once for all simulations. This combination of noise trajectories on a coarse time grid and ensemble averaging over bridge processes has practical advantages, such as a simple concatenation rule, that we highlight with numerical examples.

.
tldr: A method for temporal coarse-graining of classical stochastic noise in quantum systems, focusing on Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.
motivation: Simulating quantum systems with temporally correlated classical noise (e.g., 1/f noise) is computationally challenging; the paper aims to reduce complexity by integrating out high-frequency noise components.
method: The noise is expressed as a sum of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, then conditioned on a coarse realization; the ensemble average over bridge processes is performed analytically, allowing precomputation of noise propagators.
result: The deterministic components capture all dependence on the coarse realization, and the bridge processes are independent with analytically known correlators, enabling efficient simulation.
conclusion: The approach provides a practical and efficient way to simulate quantum systems with classical stochastic noise, with advantages like a simple concatenation rule.

title: Simulating Magic State Cultivation With Few Clifford Terms
authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Zhenghao Zhong, And Ainhoa Zapirain
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2134 (2026).

Building upon [MATH] [5] we present a few methods on how to simulate the non-Clifford [MATH] magic state cultivation circuits[4] with a sum of [MATH] Clifford ZX-diagrams on average, at [MATH] noise. Compared to a magic cat state stabiliser decomposition of all [MATH] non-Clifford spiders ([MATH] terms required), this is more than [MATH] times reduction in the number of terms. Our stabiliser decomposition has the advantage of representing the final non-Clifford state (in light of circuit errors) as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams. This will be useful in simulating the escape stage of magic state cultivation, where one needs to port the resultant state of cultivation into a larger Clifford circuit with many more qubits. Still, it's necessary to only track [MATH] Clifford terms. Our result sheds light on the simulability of operationally relevant, high [MATH]-count quantum circuits with some internal structure. Finally, we provide numerical results for full non-Clifford stabiliser rank simulation based on [MATH] along with optimisations using our cutting decompositions. Nearly [MATH] shots per second can be obtained on a laptop for the smaller [MATH] circuits at uniform circuit level noise [MATH], making it only [MATH][MATH] times slower than its (circuit-unspecific and un-optimised) fully Clifford proxy simulation via [MATH] using [MATH] gates.

.
tldr: This paper presents methods to simulate magic state cultivation circuits using a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, achieving a significant reduction in the number of terms compared to standard stabiliser decompositions.
motivation: Magic state cultivation is a key technique for fault-tolerant quantum computing, but simulating the non-Clifford components is computationally expensive. The authors aim to reduce the simulation cost by exploiting the structure of cultivation circuits.
method: The authors develop stabiliser decompositions that represent the non-Clifford state as a sum of Clifford ZX-diagrams, leveraging cutting techniques from prior work. They also provide optimisations for numerical simulation.
result: They achieve more than a 1000-fold reduction in the number of terms compared to a naive stabiliser decomposition, enabling nearly 1000 shots per second on a laptop for small circuits at uniform noise.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that operationally relevant high T-count circuits with internal structure can be simulated efficiently, which is useful for the escape stage of magic state cultivation.

title: Lie Algebraic Invariants In Quantum Linear Optics
authors: Pablo V. Parellada, Vicent Gimeno I Garcia, Julio José Moyano-Fernández, And Juan Carlos Garcia-Escartin
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2132 (2026).

Quantum linear optics without post-selection is not powerful enough to produce any quantum state from a given input state. This limits its utility since some applications require entangled resources that are difficult to prepare. Thus, a deeper understanding of linear optical state preparation is needed. In this work, we give a recipe to derive conserved quantities in the evolution of arbitrary states along any possible passive linear interferometer. One example of such an invariant is the spectrum of a density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra of passive linear optical Hamiltonians. These invariants give necessary conditions for exact state preparation: if the input and output states have different invariants, it is impossible to design a passive linear interferometer that evolves one into the other. Moreover, we provide a lower bound to the distance between an output and target state based on the distance between their invariants. This gives a necessary condition for approximate or heralded state preparations. Therefore, the invariants allow us to narrow the search when trying to prepare useful entangled states, like NOON states, from easy-to-prepare states, like Fock states. We conclude that future exact and approximate state preparation methods will need to consider the necessary conditions given by our invariants to weed out impossible linear optical evolutions.

.
tldr: Derives Lie algebraic invariants for passive linear optical networks that constrain state preparation.
motivation: Passive linear optics without post-selection cannot prepare arbitrary quantum states, limiting applications that require entangled resources.
method: Identifies conserved quantities (e.g., spectrum of density matrix mapped onto the Lie algebra) that remain invariant under any passive linear interferometer evolution.
result: Provides necessary conditions for exact state preparation and a lower bound on distance for approximate preparation, enabling elimination of impossible evolutions.
conclusion: Future state preparation methods must consider these invariants to avoid impossible linear optical evolutions.

title: Efficient Classical Computation Of The Neural Tangent Kernel Of Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Anderson Melchor Hernandez, Davide Pastorello, And Giacomo de Palma
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2118 (2026).

We propose an efficient classical algorithm to estimate the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) associated with a broad class of quantum neural networks. These networks consist of arbitrary unitary operators belonging to the Clifford group interleaved with parametric gates given by the time evolution generated by an arbitrary Hamiltonian belonging to the Pauli group. The proposed algorithm leverages a key insight: the average over the distribution of initialization parameters in the NTK definition can be exactly replaced by an average over just four discrete values, chosen such that the corresponding parametric gates are Clifford operations. This reduction enables an efficient classical simulation of the circuit. Combined with recent results establishing the equivalence between wide quantum neural networks and Gaussian processes [Girardi et al., Comm. Math. Phys. 406, 92 (2025); Melchor Hernandez et al., Ann. Henri Poincaré (2025)], our method enables efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, and therefore shows that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.

.
tldr: Proposes an efficient classical algorithm to compute the Neural Tangent Kernel of quantum neural networks, showing that such networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether quantum neural networks can provide a quantum advantage by analyzing their training dynamics via the Neural Tangent Kernel.
method: Replaces the average over initialization parameters in the NTK with an average over four discrete Clifford operations, enabling efficient classical simulation.
result: The algorithm allows efficient computation of the expected output of wide, trained quantum neural networks, proving that these networks cannot achieve quantum advantage.
conclusion: Wide quantum neural networks with Clifford+Pauli gates are classically simulable and thus do not offer a quantum advantage.

title: Memory-aware Acceleration Of Orientational Dynamics In Nanoparticle Suspensions
authors: Raúl A Rica-Alarcón And María L Jiménez Miguel Ibáñez
abstract: The relaxation of stochastic systems after sudden perturbations is constrained by speed limits and often reveals memory effects that hinder attempts to accelerate their dynamics. Here we demonstrate Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in the electro-orientation of non-spherical nanoparticles and show how this memory effect limits simple acceleration protocols. Experimentally, the orientational dynamics is monitored optically through field-induced birefringence, which is proportional to the nematic order parameter. When an AC electric field is first set to an extreme value until the birefringence reaches its target and is then switched to the target field (matched two-step protocol), the relaxation exhibits a characteristic Kovacs shoulder. We interpret this behavior within a theoretical framework based on the Smoluchowski equation for the orientational probability density. In the high-frequency AC regime, orientational relaxation is governed by induced dipoles, and the observed memory effect originates from polydispersity, which generates a spectrum of rotational diffusion coefficients and hence multiscale relaxation. Building on this insight, we design protocols that mitigate the detrimental effect of memory by sequentially suppressing the slowest active relaxation mode. Experiments on nanoparticle suspensions with different properties confirm these mechanisms, and we demonstrate substantial reductions in relaxation time compared with single quenches and matched two-step protocols with NaMt suspensions. More broadly, these results illustrate how memory effects emerge when many degrees of freedom are steered with a single control parameter and provide an experimentally accessible strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.
tldr: This paper demonstrates Kovacs-type nonmonotonic relaxation in nanoparticle suspensions and designs protocols to accelerate relaxation by mitigating memory effects.
motivation: Understanding and accelerating relaxation in stochastic systems is important for controlling multiscale dynamics, but memory effects often hinder simple acceleration protocols.
method: The authors use optical birefringence to monitor orientational dynamics of nanoparticles under AC electric fields, and interpret results using the Smoluchowski equation. They design multi-step protocols that sequentially suppress slow relaxation modes.
result: They observe Kovacs shoulders in two-step protocols and achieve substantial reductions in relaxation time using their designed protocols.
conclusion: Memory effects in polydisperse systems can be mitigated by tailored multi-step protocols, providing a strategy for controlling multiscale stochastic dynamics.

title: Comment On "Fundamental Limit Of Phonon Tesla Valve For Heat Rectification From First Principles"
authors: Aleksei Sokolov Samuel Huberman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28407v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Thermal rectification is a two-terminal property: the same device must carry different heat-current magnitudes when two reservoir temperatures are interchanged. In this Comment on Ref.~, we ask whether the reported ratio [MATH] can represent such a two-terminal rectification ratio within the fixed-background linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation (BTE) used in that work. We show that, for a passive two-terminal reservoir problem, any fixed linearized BTE whose scattering operator preserves a uniform equilibrium temperature shift, and whose boundary-value problem is well posed, gives equal forward and reverse resistance magnitudes. A direction-dependent response can still occur under a prescribed gradient-weighted source--sink protocol, but such a response should be distinguished from two-terminal thermal rectification.
tldr: This comment argues that the linearized phonon Boltzmann transport equation cannot produce two-terminal thermal rectification, contradicting a previous claim.
motivation: To correct a misinterpretation of thermal rectification in phononic systems and clarify the fundamental limits of heat rectification.
method: The authors analyze the linearized phonon BTE with fixed background, showing that for a passive two-terminal reservoir problem, forward and reverse resistances are equal due to symmetry of the scattering operator.
result: Any fixed linearized BTE with a scattering operator preserving uniform equilibrium temperature shift yields equal forward and reverse resistance magnitudes, so the reported rectification ratio is not a true two-terminal rectification.
conclusion: The claimed phonon Tesla valve does not demonstrate two-terminal thermal rectification within the linearized BTE framework; direction-dependent response under a gradient-weighted source-sink protocol should be distinguished from true rectification.

title: Kinetics Of Electron-phonon Scattering In Silicon Resolved By Rydberg Transitions Of Donors
authors: Nils Dessmann, Aidan G. Mcconnell, Sergey G. Pavlov, Guy Matmon, Gabriel Aeppli, Nikolay V. Abrosimov, Hari Paudyal, Michael E. Flatt\'e, Benedict N. Murdin
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28893v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rydberg states of atoms in vacuum are now well recognized as a resource for quantum technologies. Donors in semiconductors also display analogous states, which have been proposed for similar applications. While they benefit from permanent locations in their host crystals, electron-lattice coupling leads to much shorter excited-state lifetimes than for neutral atoms in vacuum. Here we provide a quantitative description of donor-phonon kinetics, creating a basis for engineering donor systems in realistic material stacks for quantum devices. Our theory incorporates both form factors for the Rydberg states, which given their large extents in real space provide strong selectivity in momentum space, and tabulated deformation potentials for all six phonon branches throughout the Brillouin zone. By confronting this framework with carefully controlled time-resolved free electron laser measurements, we show that the widely quoted position of the silicon conduction band minimum, [MATH], is inconsistent with observed donor relaxation rates and that quantitative agreement is obtained for a value further from the X-point than commonly assumed. This stringent experiment-theory comparison establishes donor relaxation as a precision metrology for conduction band parameters and scattering processes in silicon, with consequences spanning from quantum devices to classical electronics.
tldr: This paper studies electron-phonon scattering in silicon donors using Rydberg transitions, providing a quantitative model and experimental validation.
motivation: Donors in semiconductors are proposed for quantum technologies, but electron-lattice coupling shortens excited-state lifetimes; understanding phonon kinetics is essential for engineering donor-based quantum devices.
method: The authors develop a theory incorporating form factors for Rydberg states and tabulated deformation potentials for all phonon branches, and compare with time-resolved free electron laser measurements.
result: The widely quoted conduction band minimum position is inconsistent with observed relaxation rates; a value further from the X-point yields quantitative agreement.
conclusion: Donor relaxation can serve as precision metrology for conduction band parameters and scattering processes in silicon, impacting quantum devices and classical electronics.

title: Dissipative Phase Transition Of Interacting Nonreciprocal Fermions

While nonreciprocal couplings are ubiquitous in classical systems, their impact on quantum many-body criticality and entanglement remains largely unexplored. Using exact numerical simulations, we study an interacting fermionic chain subject to nonreciprocal gain and loss. We show that the interplay …


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250403] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies a dissipative phase transition in an interacting fermionic chain with nonreciprocal gain and loss, focusing on criticality and entanglement.
motivation: Nonreciprocal couplings are common in classical systems but their effect on quantum many-body criticality and entanglement is largely unexplored.
method: Exact numerical simulations of an interacting fermionic chain with nonreciprocal gain and loss.
result: The interplay of nonreciprocity and interactions leads to a dissipative phase transition with distinct entanglement properties.

title: Crystalline Spectral Form Factors
authors: Dmitrii A. Trunin And David A. Huse
abstract:
Author(s): Dmitrii A. Trunin and David A. Huse

We investigate crystallinelike behavior of the spectral form factor in unitary quantum systems with extremely strong eigenvalue repulsion. Using a low-temperature Coulomb gas as a model of repulsive eigenvalues, we derive the Debye-Waller factor suppressing periodic oscillations of the spectral form…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250405] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: The paper studies crystalline spectral form factors in quantum systems with strong eigenvalue repulsion, using a Coulomb gas model.

result: The spectral form factor exhibits a crystalline structure with suppressed oscillations, analogous to Debye-Waller factor in solids.
conclusion: The work provides a new perspective on spectral statistics in strongly repulsive quantum systems, linking to crystallinelike behavior.

title: Superbunching From Coherently Driven Atoms In A Waveguide
authors: Zeidan Zeidan, Therese Karmstrand, Maryam Khanahmadi, And Göran Johansson
abstract:
Author(s): Zeidan Zeidan, Therese Karmstrand, Maryam Khanahmadi, and Göran Johansson

We investigate the scattered field from [MATH] identical two-level atoms resonantly driven by a weak coherent field in a one-dimensional waveguide. For atoms separated by the drive wavelength, increasing the number of atoms suppresses transmission while enhancing photon bunching. Transmission becomes a…


[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 250803] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: Coherently driven atoms in a waveguide exhibit superbunching and suppressed transmission due to collective effects.
motivation: Understanding photon statistics from driven atomic ensembles is fundamental for quantum optics and waveguide QED.
method: The authors theoretically study N identical two-level atoms coupled to a 1D waveguide, driven by a weak coherent field, and compute the second-order correlation function g^(2)(0).

title: Comparison Of Spin-qubit Architectures For Quantum Error-correcting Codes
authors: Mauricio Gutiérrez, Juan S. Rojas-Arias, David Obando, And Chien-Yuan Chang
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio Gutiérrez, Juan S. Rojas-Arias, David Obando, and Chien-Yuan Chang

We investigate the performance of two quantum error-correcting codes—the surface code and the Bacon-Shor code—for implementation with spin qubits in silicon. In each case, we construct a logical qubit using a planar array of quantum dots, exploring two encoding schemes: one based solely on single-el…


[Phys. Rev. A 113, 062464] Published Fri Jun 26, 2026.
tldr: Compares surface code and Bacon-Shor code performance for spin qubits in silicon, focusing on error correction thresholds and resource overhead.
motivation: To evaluate which quantum error-correcting code is more suitable for spin qubit platforms, considering realistic noise models and physical constraints.
method: Constructs logical qubits using planar quantum dot arrays with two encoding schemes (single-electron and singlet-triplet), and simulates error correction under depolarizing and amplitude damping noise.
result: The surface code achieves higher error thresholds and lower logical error rates than the Bacon-Shor code for both encoding schemes, though the Bacon-Shor code requires fewer physical qubits.
conclusion: The surface code is preferable for spin qubit architectures when error correction performance is prioritized, while the Bacon-Shor code may be advantageous for resource-limited settings.

title: Learning Variational Quantum Circuit Parameters With Classical Artificial Intelligence For Quantum Phase Transition Detection

Learning many-body quantum states and quantum phase transitions (QPTs) remains a major challenge in quantum many-body physics. Classical machine-learning methods offer certain advantages in addressing these difficulties. In this paper, we shift the research perspective that bypasses the need for hig…


[Phys. Rev. B 113, 235157] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.

result: The approach successfully identifies phase transition points in benchmark models with reduced quantum resource requirements.
conclusion: Classical AI can assist VQC optimization for phase transition detection, but the contribution is incremental and not a core information-theoretic result.

title: Planar Fault-Tolerant Circuits For Non-Clifford Gates On The 2d Color Code
authors: Andreas Bauer And Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente
abstract:
Author(s): Andreas Bauer and Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente

A family of scalable circuits designed for universal quantum computing on planar chips with nearest-neighbor couplings called twisted color circuits is introduced and can achieve fault tolerance with a “just-in-time” decoder.

motivation: Fault-tolerant universal quantum computing requires efficient non-Clifford gates, which are challenging on planar architectures with nearest-neighbor couplings.
method: Proposes twisted color circuits, a family of scalable circuits designed for planar chips, combined with a just-in-time decoder to achieve fault tolerance.
result: Demonstrates that the proposed circuits can implement non-Clifford gates fault-tolerantly on the 2D color code with a planar layout.
conclusion: The work provides a practical path toward universal fault-tolerant quantum computing on planar chips, though it focuses on hardware-level error correction rather than information-theoretic results.

title: Quantifying Robustness And Locality Of Majorana Bound States In Interacting Systems
authors: William Samuelson, Juan Daniel Torres Luna, Sebastian Miles, A. Mert Bozkurt, Martin Leijnse, Michael Wimmer, And Viktor Svensson
abstract:

Motivated by recent quantum-dot experiments, this work rigorously defines Majorana bound states in interacting systems to quantify their protection and feasibility for non-Abelian braiding.

tldr: This paper rigorously defines Majorana bound states in interacting quantum-dot systems and quantifies their robustness and locality for non-Abelian braiding.
motivation: Recent quantum-dot experiments suggest Majorana bound states may exist, but their protection and feasibility for topological quantum computing in interacting systems need rigorous quantification.
method: The authors develop theoretical criteria to define Majorana bound states in interacting systems and compute measures of robustness and locality using numerical simulations.
result: They provide quantitative bounds on the robustness and locality of Majorana bound states, showing how interactions affect their topological protection.
conclusion: The work clarifies conditions under which Majorana bound states can be used for non-Abelian braiding, guiding experimental efforts in topological quantum computing.

title: Abelian Multi-Cycle Codes For Single-Shot Error Correction
authors: Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, And Leonid P. Pryadko
abstract:
Author(s): Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, and Leonid P. Pryadko

A new family of quantum low-density parity-check codes, which are locally equivalent to higher-dimensional hypergraph-product codes, achieves single-shot fault tolerance and an approximately 1.1% pseudothreshold with significantly shorter block lengths.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020326] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a new family of quantum LDPC codes that achieve single-shot fault tolerance with improved pseudothreshold and shorter block lengths.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum error correction typically requires multiple rounds of syndrome measurement, which is resource-intensive. Single-shot error correction reduces this overhead by using redundant syndrome information.
method: The authors construct Abelian multi-cycle codes, which are locally equivalent to higher-dimensional hypergraph-product codes, and analyze their single-shot error correction capabilities using belief propagation and ordered statistics decoding.
result: The codes achieve a pseudothreshold of approximately 1.1% with significantly shorter block lengths compared to previous single-shot codes.
conclusion: Abelian multi-cycle codes offer a practical advantage for fault-tolerant quantum computing by enabling single-shot error correction with moderate overhead.

title: Squeezing Enhancement In Lossy Multi-Path Atom Interferometers
authors: Julian Günther, Jan-Niclas Kirsten-Siemß, Naceur Gaaloul, And Klemens Hammerer
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2122 (2026).

This paper explores the sensitivity gains afforded by spin-squeezed states in atom interferometry, in particular using Bragg diffraction. We introduce a generalised input-output formalism that accurately describes realistic, non-unitary interferometers, including losses due to velocity selectivity and scattering into undesired momentum states. This formalism is applied to evaluate the performance of one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states in improving phase sensitivity. Our results show that by carefully optimising the parameters of the Bragg beam splitters and controlling the degree of squeezing, it is possible to improve the sensitivity of the interferometer by several dB with respect to the standard quantum limit despite realistic levels of losses in light pulse operations. However, the analysis also highlights the challenges associated with achieving these improvements in practice, most notably the impact of finite temperature on the benefits of entanglement. The results suggest ways of optimising interferometric setups to exploit quantum entanglement under realistic conditions, thereby contributing to advances in precision metrology with atom interferometers.

.
tldr: This paper studies spin-squeezed states in lossy atom interferometers for phase sensitivity enhancement.
motivation: Atom interferometry is a key tool for precision metrology, and spin-squeezed states can surpass the standard quantum limit, but realistic losses limit their advantage.
method: The authors develop a generalized input-output formalism for non-unitary interferometers including losses from velocity selectivity and scattering, and apply it to one-axis twisted spin-squeezed states.
result: Optimizing Bragg beam splitter parameters and squeezing degree yields several dB sensitivity improvement over the standard quantum limit despite losses, but finite temperature reduces the benefit.
conclusion: Quantum entanglement can enhance atom interferometry under realistic conditions, but practical challenges like temperature must be addressed.

title: Exploring The Effects Of Entanglement On Quantum Machine Learning Of Pathogen Epitope-Receptor Binding
authors: Aspen Erlandsson Brisebois, Luis Pablo Gonzalez Dominguez, Shivansi Prajapati, Zahed Khatooni, Heather L. Wilson, Connor Burbridge, Brook Byrns, Sureesh Tikoo, Christophe Pere, Steven Rayan, Gordon Broderick
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) provide a flexible substrate for hybrid quantum machine learning (QML), but their practical value on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices remains an empirical question, especially because training depth and scale can introduce optimization challenges such as barren plateaus. Here we study how the number and topology of two-qubit entangling gates in the feature-map stage influence a fixed hybrid QNN workflow for classifying strong versus weak epitope-receptor binding in Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (PRRS) vaccine design. The dataset consists of docking-derived binding affinities for N=80 9-mer epitopes, labeled as Strong or Weak binding, and partitioned into training, validation, and test subsets using a 40:30:30 split. We compare a classical CNN benchmark with a hybrid Embedding-QNN architecture under four feature-map configurations: a non-entangling Z feature map, an all-to-all high-entanglement ZZ feature map, and two interleaved nearest-neighbour entanglement patterns of low and high depth. Among the configurations tested, the high-entanglement ZZ feature map is seen to provide the strongest evidence of reduced training-set overfit, with a lower training area under the accuracy curve (AUAC) and the highest test/training AUAC ratio, while preserving competitive test-set accuracy. These results do not establish a general QML advantage, but they suggest that feature-map entanglement topology is a meaningful design variable for sparse biological screening tasks and warrants further evaluation with additional metrics, larger datasets, and noise-aware or hardware-based experiments.
tldr: This paper explores how entanglement topology in quantum feature maps affects a hybrid quantum-classical machine learning workflow for classifying epitope-receptor binding affinities.
motivation: The study aims to understand whether entanglement in parameterized quantum circuits can improve classification performance on a small biological dataset, addressing the practical value of QML on NISQ devices.
method: A hybrid Embedding-QNN architecture is compared with a classical CNN benchmark using four feature-map configurations (non-entangling, all-to-all high-entanglement ZZ, and two nearest-neighbor entanglement patterns) on a dataset of 80 9-mer epitopes labeled as Strong or Weak binding.
result: The high-entanglement ZZ feature map showed the strongest evidence of reduced overfitting, with lower training AUAC and highest test/training AUAC ratio, while maintaining competitive test accuracy.
conclusion: Feature-map entanglement topology is a meaningful design variable for sparse biological screening tasks, but no general QML advantage is established; further evaluation with larger datasets and noise-aware experiments is needed.

title: Bipartite Gaussian Boson Sampling For Hamiltonian Cycles In Directed Graphs
authors: Miaomiao Yu, Jingyi Lv, Yan Wang, Kun Wang, Ping Xu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bipartite Gaussian boson sampling (BipartiteGBS) produces output probabilities governed by squared permanents of submatrices of arbitrary complex matrices, matching the nonsymmetric structure of directed graphs. Most GBS-based graph algorithms, however, rely on symmetric hafnian structure and are formulated for undirected problems. Here we propose a BipartiteGBS-based framework for directed-graph heuristic optimization. We introduce Max-Perm as a canonical optimization task for BipartiteGBS and derive a closed-form sampling enhancement factor relative to uniform classical sampling in this idealized setting. We then use permanent-biased BipartiteGBS samples to guide a genetic algorithm for the celebrated directed Hamiltonian cycle problem. Numerical experiments on Erds--R\'enyi random directed graphs show that the resulting BipartiteGBS-enhanced algorithms improve success rates over a standard genetic algorithm and yield longer valid paths when no Hamiltonian cycle is found, while ablation tests indicate that BipartiteGBS-guided initialization is the dominant contributor. These results show how permanent-based photonic sampling can provide useful algorithmic guidance for asymmetric combinatorial search.
tldr: This paper proposes a bipartite Gaussian boson sampling framework for directed graph optimization, specifically for the Hamiltonian cycle problem.
motivation: Most GBS-based graph algorithms are limited to undirected graphs due to symmetric hafnian structure; the authors aim to extend GBS to directed graphs using bipartite GBS.
method: They introduce Max-Perm as a canonical optimization task for bipartite GBS, derive a closed-form sampling enhancement factor, and use permanent-biased samples to guide a genetic algorithm for directed Hamiltonian cycle problems.
result: Numerical experiments on random directed graphs show improved success rates and longer valid paths compared to a standard genetic algorithm, with ablation tests indicating that GBS-guided initialization is the dominant contributor.
conclusion: Permanent-based photonic sampling can provide useful algorithmic guidance for asymmetric combinatorial search problems.

title: Properties Of 2d Electron Or Hole Gases At Tailored s-Si/SiGe Interfaces: A First-Principles Investigation
authors: Garima Ahuja, Farha S, Tanuja Shridhar Joshi, Anil Shaji, Shobhana Narasimhan
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28776v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We have performed first-principles hybrid density functional theory calculations to study the formation and properties of two-dimensional electron or hole gases (2DEG or 2DHG) at s-Si/SiGe interfaces. For small Ge concentrations [MATH], we find a novel type of band alignment with no offset in the conduction bands, implying that a 2DEG cannot be formed, though a 2DHG can. In contrast, for [MATH] the band alignment suggests that either a 2DEG or 2DHG can be formed. The electronic band structure features two nearly degenerate 2DEG states at the bottom of the conduction bands, and two 2DHG states at the top of the valence band. These states can be accessed by appropriate doping and gating. Charge density plots of these states show that they feature carriers confined to the near vicinity (2--3 atomic layers) of the interface. Calculated effective masses are anisotropic, being markedly so for the 2DHG states, and in excellent agreement with experiment. This property can be exploited to create a 1D carrier gas. Our results are especially important for s-Si/SiGe-based semiconducting spin qubits for quantum computing applications.
tldr: First-principles study of 2D electron/hole gases at s-Si/SiGe interfaces for spin qubit applications.
motivation: To understand the electronic properties of tailored s-Si/SiGe interfaces for potential use in semiconducting spin qubits.
method: Hybrid density functional theory calculations to compute band alignment, effective masses, and charge density.
result: For low Ge concentration, no 2DEG forms but a 2DHG does; for higher Ge, both can form. Effective masses are anisotropic and agree with experiment.
conclusion: The interface properties can be exploited for 1D carrier gases and are relevant for SiGe-based spin qubits.

title: Quantum Variational Approaches To The Maximum Independent Set Problem At Utility Scale
authors: Kalyan Dasgupta, Sumanta Mukherjee, Dhriti Verma, Surya Shravan Kumar Sajja, Abhishek Singh, Dzung Phan, Jayant Kalagnanam
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study variational quantum algorithms for the Maximum Independent Set (MIS) problem on benchmark graphs of 64, 99, and 180 vertices. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) and Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) are compared across SPSA and COBYLA optimizers at multiple circuit depths. A preprocessing pipeline comprising spectral graph reordering (via the Fiedler vector) and distance-based sparsification reduces circuit depth while preserving energy fidelity. Classical post-processing via history-guided bitstring correction and stepwise maximality extension recovers the exact MIS across all instances. With CVaR optimization, VQE with SPSArecovers up to 6 distinct MIS per run for the 64-node instance and up to 10 distinct MIS per run for the 99-node instance, sampling broadly from the optimal solution population. Repeated runs with different SPSA trajectories collectively enumerate a larger fraction of all MIS for each instance. For the 180-node instance, where standard approaches stall at size 14 (MIS is 15), we introduce ancilla-assisted superposition initialization: ancilla qubits prepare a uniform superposition over classically-found near-optimal solutions, and an excitation-preserving ansatz evolves this state while conserving Hamming weight. This novel construction enables quantum-parallel variational search over multiple seeds simultaneously, discovering the exact MIS where single-seed methods fail. The 180-qubit simulation represents, to our knowledge, the largest scale at which gate-based variational algorithms have solved MIS to optimality. Hardware validation on IBM Quantum hardware ibm_marrakesh confirms that converged simulator parameters transfer effectively to noisy quantum execution.
tldr: This paper applies variational quantum algorithms (VQE and QAOA) to solve the Maximum Independent Set problem on graphs up to 180 vertices, using preprocessing and ancilla-assisted initialization to achieve optimal solutions.
motivation: The Maximum Independent Set problem is a classic NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with practical applications; quantum variational algorithms may offer advantages for large instances.
method: The authors compare VQE and QAOA with SPSA and COBYLA optimizers, employ spectral graph reordering and sparsification to reduce circuit depth, use CVaR optimization and history-guided post-processing, and introduce ancilla-assisted superposition initialization for larger instances.
result: The methods recover exact MIS for all tested instances up to 180 vertices, with VQE+SPSA finding multiple distinct MIS per run; the 180-qubit simulation is the largest gate-based variational MIS solution to date.
conclusion: Variational quantum algorithms with appropriate preprocessing and initialization can solve MIS at utility scale, and parameters transfer effectively to noisy quantum hardware.

title: Reply To Comment On "Scaling And Universality At Noisy Quench Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions"
authors: S. Ansari, R. Jafari, A. Akbari, M. Abdi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Comment by J. Sirker [arXiv:2511.16509] raises an important issue concerning dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in noisy and mixed-state dynamics, namely that the extension of the Loschmidt echo from pure to mixed states is not unique and different extensions preserve different physical properties. The Comment examines a noise-averaged mixed-state fidelity and shows that DQPTs cannot occur for any nonzero noise when the return rate is defined through the Uhlmann-Bures fidelity of the noise-averaged density matrix. This conclusion is valid for the mixed-state fidelity observable discussed in the Comment and is consistent with prior studies [[URL] arXiv:2504.03005]. Our article [[URL] investigated a different operationally defined quantity: the logarithm of the Loschmidt echo obtained by first determining the noise-averaged excitation probabilities generated during the noisy ramp and then performing a coherent post-ramp evolution of a pure state constructed from these noise-averaged transition probabilities. As emphasized explicitly in our original publication, this observable is defined through an operational assumption and is not the same quantity as the mixed-state fidelity. The nonanalyticities reported in Ref. [[URL] therefore concern this two-stage operational protocol and should not be identified with zeros of the Uhlmann-Bures fidelity. There is therefore no direct contradiction between the theorem established for the Uhlmann-Bures return rate and the conclusions obtained for the different operational protocol studied in Ref. [[URL].
tldr: A reply clarifying that the nonanalyticities in a noisy quench dynamical quantum phase transition arise from an operational protocol different from the mixed-state fidelity, thus not contradicting known theorems.
motivation: To address a comment questioning the validity of dynamical quantum phase transitions in noisy mixed-state dynamics by clarifying the definition of the observable used.
method: The authors distinguish between the noise-averaged Loschmidt echo defined via an operational two-stage protocol and the Uhlmann-Bures fidelity of the noise-averaged density matrix.
result: The nonanalyticities reported are for the operational protocol and do not conflict with the theorem that DQPTs cannot occur for nonzero noise when using Uhlmann-Bures fidelity.
conclusion: There is no contradiction; the two observables are different and the conclusions apply to their respective definitions.

title: Channel Capacity Under The Subtractive Dithered Quantization Model
authors: Hossein Atrsaei, Mireille Sarkiss, Mich\`ele Wigger
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28842v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the capacity of an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel followed by a subtractive dithered uniform quantizer. Under the Schuchman conditions and with negligible overload probability, the system admits an additive-noise representation in which the effective noise is the sum of Gaussian and uniform components. Capacity bounds are derived for this model when inputs are subject to an average-power constraint as well as a peak-amplitude constraint, where the latter accounts for the limited quantizer dynamic range. Specifically, a computable lower bound is obtained based on the entropy power inequality (EPI), using the maximum-entropy input under the above constraints. Tighter numerical lower bounds are derived using discrete input constellations with finite mass points. Finally, an upper bound is obtained by exploiting the fact that Gaussian distributions maximize entropy under a variance constraint. Numerical results show that, for a K-level quantizer, discrete constellations with K mass points already achieve near-optimal rates among the tested families. Moreover, our upper bound is close to the lower bounds in the moderate-SNR regime; it thus represents a good and simple capacity approximation in this regime.
tldr: This paper studies the capacity of an AWGN channel followed by a subtractive dithered uniform quantizer, deriving bounds under power and peak-amplitude constraints.
motivation: Understanding the fundamental limits of communication through quantized channels is important for practical digital communication systems.
method: The authors use the entropy power inequality and maximum-entropy inputs to derive lower bounds, and exploit Gaussian entropy maximization for upper bounds.
result: Discrete constellations with K mass points achieve near-optimal rates for a K-level quantizer, and the upper bound is tight in the moderate-SNR regime.
conclusion: The derived bounds provide a good capacity approximation for the subtractive dithered quantization model, especially at moderate SNR.

conclusion: The work provides insights into superfluid stability but does not address information-theoretic or thermodynamic aspects relevant to the user's interests.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators

abstract:

This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. tldr: A comprehensive review of photoinduced nonequilibrium states in Mott insulators, focusing on strong electronic correlations and optical control.
motivation: To understand and control nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated materials, which may lead to novel phases and functionalities.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental advances, including dynamical mean-field theory and time-resolved spectroscopy.
result: Key mechanisms for photodoping, metastable states, and nonthermal orders (superconducting, magnetic, etc.) are identified.
conclusion: Photoexcitation offers a powerful tool to manipulate correlated materials, but the field is still developing with many open questions.

title: Schr\"odingerization Based Quantum Algorithms For Regularized Wasserstein Proximal Operators
authors: Shi Jin, Nana Liu, Yue Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28752v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a quantum algorithm for the regularized Wasserstein proximal operator, which is a fundamental tool in optimal transport and mean-field games. The regularization introduces a small diffusive term into the continuity equation of the Benamou-Brenier formulation, which results in a forward-backward PDE system consisting of a Fokker-Planck equation and a viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equation with a quadratic Hamiltonian. Through the Cole-Hopf transformation, both equations are converted to forward heat equations, whose coupling requires a Hadamard division to prepare the initial data for the second heat equation and a Hadamard product to recover the terminal density. We solve these heat equations via the Schr\"odingerization method and implement the Hadamard division and product operations using simple matrix-vector multiplication representations. The complete quantum algorithm prepares an [MATH]-approximation of the terminal density state with [MATH] query complexity, up to constants depending on the potential and initial density, where [MATH] is the spatial dimension, [MATH] is the number of grid points per spatial dimension and [MATH] is the evolution time. The complexity depends only {\it linearly} on [MATH], yielding an {\it exponential} speedup over classical methods, whose cost scales as [MATH] per time step. Numerical experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for regularized Wasserstein proximal operators using Schrödingerization, achieving exponential speedup over classical methods.
motivation: To solve optimal transport and mean-field games problems more efficiently using quantum computing.
method: Converts the PDE system into heat equations via Cole-Hopf transformation, solves them with Schrödingerization, and implements Hadamard operations with matrix-vector multiplication.
result: The algorithm achieves O(ε^{-1} N^{1/2} T) query complexity, exponential speedup over classical O(N^{3/2}) per time step.
conclusion: The proposed quantum algorithm is effective and offers significant speedup for high-dimensional problems.

title: MetaMorphQ: Physics-Based Metamorphic Testing Of Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Ngoc Nhi Nguyen, John Le, Thai T. Vu, Thi Thuy Nga Nguyen, Jun Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.28742v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) are central to quantum computing, yet testing them remains challenging due to the oracle problem: the ground-state energy they compute is itself unknown. Existing approaches, such as convergence-based testing, are unreliable and yield high false-positive rates due to optimisation instability. We propose METAMORPHQ, a metamorphic testing framework that derives test oracles directly from quantum mechanical properties of VQE circuits. Exploiting algebraic properties of parametrised rotation gates and diagonal Hamiltonians, we define five physics-based invariants that hold for any correct circuit and can be verified at initialisation without ground-truth outputs. Evaluated on 500 benchmark circuits with 2,469 mutants, METAMORPHQ achieves zero false positives and significantly improves diagnostic effectiveness (Youden's J = 0.57 vs. 0.02 for convergence testing). These results demonstrate that physics-derived invariants provide a practical, oracle-free foundation for testing quantum software, enabling reliable validation of both human- and LLM-generated circuits.
tldr: A metamorphic testing framework for variational quantum circuits using physics-based invariants.
motivation: Testing VQE circuits is challenging due to the oracle problem; existing convergence-based testing is unreliable with high false positives.
method: Derives five physics-based invariants from algebraic properties of parametrized rotation gates and diagonal Hamiltonians, verified at initialization without ground-truth outputs.
result: Evaluated on 500 benchmark circuits with 2,469 mutants, achieving zero false positives and significantly better diagnostic effectiveness (Youden's J = 0.57 vs 0.02).
conclusion: Physics-derived invariants provide a practical, oracle-free foundation for testing quantum software.
